#851. Rosie O’Donnell Slams Megyn Kelly for Defending Russell Brand

Rosie O’Donnell put Megyn Kelly on blast after the Fox News alum said she "didn't believe" the rape and sexual assault charges against Russell Brand, who's been sentenced to 10.5 years in prison.

Rosie O'Donnell has heated words for Megyn Kelly.

The View alum put the former Fox News anchor on blast for defending Russell Brand after he was sentenced to 10.5 years in prison on rape and sexual assault charges in the the United Kingdom.

Commenting under a post featuring Kelly's words of support for Brand, O'Donnell wrote on Threads Nov. 9, "Go f--k urself Megan."

Kelly has been open about her disapproval on the trial against Brand. During the Nov. 9 episode of her eponymous SiriusXM radio show, the 55-year-old called the verdict "an outrage."

“I don’t believe the charges,” she said, “and I don’t have to believe them just because the jury came through with the opposite conclusion.”

Kelly continued, "If you were to read the articles about Russell's case, his verdict and his sentencing over the past three days, it is clear that they are treating him like he is one of the most prolific sexual predators ever to roam the earth."

Brand’s legal battle began in 2025, when he was charged with two counts count of rape, one count of oral rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault for alleged incidents spanning between 1999 and 2009.

At the time, the comedian—a dad to three kids with wife Laura Brand—shared a video to social media urging the public “to understand the truth of my situation and scenario."

“I pray Lord, anyone that I’ve harmed or hurt in my years of mindlessness and sin would be healed, Lord,” he said. “And I pray, Lord, for the absolute truth of who I am to be abundantly revealed.”

During the trial, Brand—who had pleaded not guilty to all charges—did not deny that some of the encounters had occurred, though he claimed every act had been consensual.

A London jury found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Nov. 5 following eight hours of deliberation. The Get Him to the Greek star was cleared of two separate counts of rape and one count of indecent assault.

For a deeper look into Brand's trial, keep reading...

Russell Brand was charged with rape and sexual assault in April 2025.

The London Metropolitan Police charged Brand for one count of rape, two counts of indecent assault and one count of indecent assault in April 2025 for events that transpired between 1999 and 2005.

At the time, Brand immediately denied the allegations in a video response, noting he was receiving “egregious attacks” from the media in addition to the allegations.

“Amidst this litany of astonishing, rather baroque attacks are some very serious allegations,” Brand said in a video shared to social media at the time, “that I absolutely refute.”

Russell Brand pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Though the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star had previously written in a 2007 essay for The Guardian that he had a “sexy addiction” and “disregard for social conventions of sexual protocol,” he vehemently denied the charges against him.

In his video statement, Brand admitted he had been a “fool” in the past, although maintained he never partook in “non-consensual activity.”

“I was a fool before I lived in the light of the Lord,” Brand said in a video shared to his X account in April 2025. “I was a drug addict, a sex addict and an imbecile, but what I never was, was a rapist.”

In the same video, Brand noted he was “grateful” to have the opportunity to fight the allegations in court.  He pleaded not guilty to all five charges in May 2025.

Russell Brand was served with two more sexual offense charges in December 2025.

In December 2025, the London Metropolitan Police charged Brand with one additional count of rape and one additional count of sexual assault regarding incidents that took place with two separate women in 2009.

Brand responded to the charges in a separate video posted to his social media.

“I pray Lord, anyone that I’ve harmed or hurt in my years of mindlessness and sin would be healed, Lord,” he said in the clip. “And I pray, Lord, for the absolute truth of who I am to be abundantly revealed.”

With the additional allegations, Brand was charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault involving six women for events that transpired between 1999 and 2009. He later pleaded not guilty to the additional charges.

Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

In a November 2026 ruling, a London court found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was cleared of two additional counts of rape and one count of indecent assault.

During the trial, Brand maintained his innocence and said that while he dedicated much of his life to “beyond reckless philandering,” per the New York Times, he never engaged in non-consensual activities.

Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison.

After confirming he would sentence the Get Him to the Greek alum with “significant custodial time,” during the ruling and denying him bail, presiding judge Joel Bennathan sentenced Brand to 10 years and six months in prison.

During the Nov. 9, 2026 sentencing, Bennathan called Brand a “sexual predator,” and commended the women who testified for their “determination and bravery.”

Bennathan said he considered Brand’s family in his ruling, calling his decision a “sad loss” for Brand’s three children, whom he shares with wife Laura Brand.

However, the judge noted that Brand had brought the decision “upon himself,” noting the comedian had acted with “casual, arrogant disregard,” for women.

Russell Brand legal team said he is a “fundamentally different person” now.

Prior to the sentencing, Brand’s lawyer Ian Winter KC said his client is “fundamentally a different person today,” than he was when the incidents took place, per CBS News.

Winter noted that the rape for which Brand was found guilty—which took place in 2009—was a “momentary total failure.”

Brand is also represented by Oliver Schneider-Sikorsky. His legal team will have the opportunity to appeal.

Life can leave its mark on a planetary atmosphere, so learning what properties are the product of non-life will help astronomers identify those worlds that might have life.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe.

Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.

To aid in distinguishing between habitable and inhabited planets, planetary scientist Samantha Gilbert-Janizek of the University of California, Riverside, developed a model that simulates the evolution of a rocky planet without life.

"The model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets," Gilbert-Janizek, who was a PhD student at the University of Washington when the research was conducted, said in a statement.

Gilbert-Janizek built upon a model previously developed by Washington’s Rory Barnes that simulated the core, mantle, and crust of a planet. This new model pushed the simulation two steps further by incorporating the surface and atmosphere of the planet as well.

In all, the model simulates 19 properties of a rocky planet that are not related to life, including the amount of heat a planet receives from its star, the exchange of heat and chemicals from the core to the surface, and the outflow of certain gases from the subsurface.

Gilbert-Janizek’s starting point was to simulate the development of Earth had life never arisen here, therefore providing a baseline with which to compare to exoplanets. She ran the simulation from the birth of Earth 4.5 billion years ago to 500 million years into the future. The result was a lifeless world, but one that still had oceans and an atmosphere.

"When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface," said Gilbert-Janizek.

What makes the simulation especially useful is its plug-and-play nature. Researchers can simply apply the bulk properties of whichever planet they are studying to the model, and then just let it run. If the result is a planet with an atmosphere that matches what is detected spectroscopically by the James Webb Space Telescope or, in the future, the various extremely large 30-meter-plus ground-based telescopes or NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, then we know that planet probably does not have life as we know it.

However, if the simulated planet without life does not match what we observe on the real planet, then it becomes possible that life is present and altering the atmosphere.

"Dr Gilbert-Janizek’s work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,” said Barnes. "After more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earth’s core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate."

While any deviation from what is predicted by the model will not necessarily mean there is definitely life on a planet, it will help pick out those worlds that are worthy of follow-up studies by the next generation of telescopes.

Gilbert-Janizek’s model is described in a paper published in The Planetary Science Journal.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#849. Daily briefing: Should old, bad science be culled from the literature?

Physicists used an algorithm to combine telescope measurements of a black hole in a different way from the original analysis.Credit: S. Lai, N. Thyagarajan, O. I. Wong and F. Diakogiannis/CSIRO

A re-evaluation of data from the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has corroborated the findings that yielded the first-ever photo of a black hole. After the blurry image was released in 2019, sceptics argued that the circular shape seen in the shot was an artefact of the team’s image-reconstruction techniques. Independent astrophysicist Samuel Lai and his team used different methods to reanalyse the original data and their results — including new images of the black hole — largely match those of the EHT team.

The funding that voters in California have approved to earmark for immunology research — the largest ever infusion of cash for science authorized by a public vote in US history. (Nature | 5 min read)

Researchers have catalogued almost 100 proteins that get a free pass through the blood–brain barrier to maintain the health of neurons. Most of these proteins were produced in distant organs, particularly the liver. The team found that the transport of some of these proteins is disrupted in mice with a brain disease that mimics early-stage Alzheimer’s disease. The work suggests that the brain actively imports the proteins it needs to stay healthy, and that the breakdown of that transport drives the dysfunction seen in neurodegenerative disease, says neuroscientist and study co-author Andrew Yang.

The launch of the Artemis II mission to orbit the Moon produced unprecedented large-scale atmospheric disturbances, say researchers. Data from GPS receivers found that the Space Launch System — the most powerful rocket that NASA has ever built — disrupted the atmospheric layer known as the ionosphere. The GPS disruption was potentially large enough to “have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning,” says space physicist and study co-author Charles Lin.

Reference: Geophysical Research Letters preprint (not peer reviewed)

The scientific literature contains decades-old papers that detail fraudulent, unethical or merely incorrect results, but aren’t marked as such. Many of these papers are long neglected, but their digitization enables artificial-intelligence tools that summarize scientific literature on a topic to feed misinformation to a new generation. This leaves publishers to wrangle with the question of whether these historical papers should be retracted or flagged as suspect — a task that can be tricky if authors are dead, original records can’t be consulted or journals are no longer in print.

“You need a container before you can get the chemistry” that enables cellular life, says astrobiologist Bruce Damer. He’s among those researchers who favour a ‘lipid-first’ hypothesis for the origin of complex life: that the lipid membrane that corrals the cell is key to its success. Or even that bubbles of lipids, plus the chemistry they enclosed, could have propagated and evolved in a Darwinian-like way, before RNA (or DNA) arrived on the scene.

Enjoy more ideas about where we came from in Quanta Magazine’s Origins of Life Week.

Social scientists should be involved in the process of finding suitable locations for new observatories, argues anthropologist Jaco de Swart, co-principal investigator of a proposed neutrino detector to be built in the Peruvian Andes. Many suitable locations for such projects are sensitive ecological environments with cultural significance for Indigenous communities. Social scientists can help to integrate environmental care into these projects and build relationships with local and Indigenous stakeholders. “To build scientific infrastructure that is responsible, just and resilient, humanities scholars must have leadership roles from the start,” de Swart writes.

Appearing in the Jurassic Park franchise is the strongest predictor of a dinosaur species’ popularity, according to new research — an example of the ‘blockbuster effect’. The media should leverage this effect to put a spotlight on endangered species, says zoologist Pâmela Lima. (Science | 7 min read)

#848. ‘Second ball’ may be a Sunday league mantra but Yates showed its top-flight relevance

Midfielder’s old-school attributes came to the fore during Nottingham Forest’s win against Manchester City

Modern football is more systematised and data-driven than ever but some things never change. Winning the first ball is important but the second ball – the holy grail for Sunday league footballers – is often more so.

Nottingham Forest’s 3-1 win against Manchester City last weekend featured a classic example. Forest led 2-1 inside the last 20 minutes but City, lifted by Rayan Cherki’s sweet half-volley, were pushing for an equaliser.

Another City attack comes down their right: after Jair Cunha’s clearing header from a deep Matheus Nunes cross, the ball loops up in the air before descending inside the home penalty area.

Ryan Yates, Forest’s old-fashioned midfield general, is being pressed from behind by the Argentina international Enzo Fernández as the ball drops. Yates stands his ground, using his strength to hold off his opponent’s muscular challenge. Fernández tries to impose himself, too, but ends up on the turf.

Not only does Yates win that crucial one-on-one, by cleverly improvising an overhead kick to shift the ball away from danger he inadvertently begins a counterattack that arguably changes the course of Forest’s season.

Liam Delap shepherds the ball to Morgan Gibbs-White. Enzo Maresca’s team are hopelessly exposed and Gibbs-White devours the space in front of him with a driving run.

He lays a pass off to Delap, who takes one touch before swerving a sensational shot into the far corner for 3-1. It is a memorable move that will surely compete for goal of the month. But none of it would have been possible without the dirty work of Yates: a show of strength and desire from the captain at the other end of the pitch.

Oliver Glasner understands the importance of the moment and sprints to celebrate with his players. After a barren scoring run Delap suddenly has two goals in one afternoon. The home fans are delirious. Twelve seconds after Yates won the duel, Forest have a two-goal cushion rather than a desperate fight to maintain their lead.

The second ball is a pleasingly old-school term but remains of paramount importance. Visit your local amateur club and you are likely to hear it being shouted as a motivational mantra.

At grassroots level it’s a reminder to teammates that finesse and creativity are all very well, but it’s hard work, desire and a refusal to let your opponent get the better of you that win matches.

And it remains part of the elite game’s lexicon. Premier League managers sometimes point to upcoming opponents’ second-ball prowess – a back-handed compliment if ever there was one. The hidden meaning: “They feed off scraps at set pieces. They don’t create from open play.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

After seeing Southampton Under-21s lose to Wealdstone in the National League Cup a couple of years ago, I mentioned to the then Saints manager, Simon Rusk, that his goalkeeper had been shouting “second ball” throughout.

“To be honest,” Rusk replied with amusing frankness, “I’m not sure some of them even know what second ball means.”

Managers like relying on data. They like predictable outcomes. They prefer to remove risk, reduce chaos and exert control over as much of the game as possible. But while the outcome of a one-on-one duel can never be certain, the consequences can often be far-reaching. That’s why second balls matter.

Against City Yates was named in Forest’s starting lineup, and given the captain’s armband, for the first time this season. Glasner, asked how he had motivated his players, revealed: “Ryan Yates spoke. I played more than 500 games as a player, I’ve managed, I don’t know, 500 games … and I’ve never heard such an inspiring speech.”

Glasner’s captain backed up stirring words with action. If there was a sense Yates’s star was fading – that his attributes of graft, tenacity and box-to-box drive were losing currency – then it was emphatically extinguished at the City Ground.

Win the first one if you can. But it’s the second ball that often makes the difference.

#846. How Patrick Mahomes Wants to "Even the Score" With Baby No. 4

After Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes revealed she is pregnant with baby No. 4, the Kansas City Chiefs star—dad to two daughters and a son with his wife—teased his hopes to “even the score.”

Patrick Mahomes knows who he wants to draft to his team.

The day after the Kansas City Chiefs quarterback and his wife Brittany Mahomes announced they are expecting their fourth baby, he admitted he’d love to see another boy join him and 3-year-old son Bronze in the huddle.

“Obviously it’s a blessing to have another baby on the way. I’m excited for it,” Patrick said during a Nov. 11 press conference. “I’m hoping that me and Bronze can even up the score.”

But while he may have a route he’s aiming for, the 31-year-old—also dad to daughters Sterling, 5, and Golden, 21 months, with Brittany—would be just as happy with a baby girl. As he put it, “I’m just praying for a healthy baby at the end of the day.”

Meanwhile, the three-time Super Bowl champ sees his expanding family roster as motivation to continue growing his football team’s winning record this season.

“I’m hoping that we can keep that [success] going and get another Super Bowl win with a baby on the way,” Patrick added. “That’d be awesome, for sure.”

While the athlete has certainly found success on the field since being drafted in the first round by the Chiefs in 2017, he has explained that his role as quarterback to his kids has improved his game play.

"You learn a ton being a father, man,” he told reporters ahead of the 2024 Super Bowl, per KSL Sports. “You learn how to be patient."

"You learn how to try to really boost people’s confidence, especially your kids,” Patrick added. “Through seasons like I’ve had this last year, it’s never losing hope, never going too negative in adverse times. Just continue to boost people’s confidence, continue to strive for hard work and really be patient."

The three-headed Kaiju's origins aren't just space-based; one of the largest structures in the universe shares its name.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Godzilla goes toe-to-toe with long-time foe King Ghidorah in Godzilla Minus Zero, which opened in theaters on Friday (Nov. 6). Though the three-headed golden Kaiju might seem like a natural native of Monster Island, King Ghidorah actually emerged from the depths of space.

However, it isn't just the origins of King Ghidorah — also known as Monster Zero in the Godzilla movie Invasion of Astro-Monster (1965) — that are this beast's only cosmic connection. One of the largest structures in the universe, the King Ghidorah Supercluster, was named in honor of Godzilla's primary antagonist.

King Ghidorah is a three-headed, twin-tailed golden dragon from the stars, first introduced in the fifth Godzilla movie, Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster (1964).

In this first appearance, part of the Shōwa era (1964–1975) of Godzilla history, Ghidorah ravaged Venus, wiping out its population 5,000 years before arriving on Earth encased within a highly magnetic meteorite. Ghidorah was bested this first time by Godzilla, Rodan, and Mothra.

Undeterred, Ghidorah returned for a rematch just a year later in Invasion of Astro Monster (1965), after being discovered supposedly terrorizing the inhabitants of Planet X, a world found beyond Jupiter. In this movie, it is revealed that Ghidorah is less a king and more a pawn, under the control of calculating Xiliens as part of a plan to subjugate Earth. This will become a theme.

Freed from that control, Ghidorah returns to deep space, once again falling under the thrall of an alien race in 1968's Destroy All Monsters.This movie sees Ghidorah hold its own against a who's who of kaiju, eventually succumbing to the combined might of Godzilla, Minilla, Mothra, Rodan, Manda, Gorosaurus, Anguirus, Kumonga, Baragon, and Varan.

Even with three gravity-beam-blasting heads, that is hardly fair!

Ghidorah returned with some backup for a final time in the Shōwa era in 1975's Godzilla vs. Gigan. This time, Ghidorah and his tag-team partner Gigan (who resembled a giant one-eyed space chicken) were under the control of cockroach-like Nebulans. Getting mind-controlled three times is just embarrassing!

Fortunately, the Shōwa era drew to a close in 1975 before Ghidorah was forced into servitude for a fourth time.

Ghidorah returned in the rebooted Godzilla timeline of the Heisei era (1991–1998) in 1991's Godzilla Vs. King Ghidorah, but its cosmic origins are gone. The Heisei Ghidorah begins life as three genetically engineered creatures called Dorats in the future before being morphed into a three-headed form via nuclear exposure.

Ghidorah was given a spiritual origin in the Millennium era's Godzilla, Mothra, and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack (2001), actually serving as a protagonist, helping Mothra in halting Godzilla's rampage.

Ghidorah is once again an extraterrestrial in Universal Pictures' MonsterVerse movie Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019), being described as having "fallen from the stars" in ancient times before rising to challenge Godzilla.

Now King Ghidorah is back once again in Godzilla Minus Zero, maintaining his extraterrestrial origin story and once again challenging Godzilla to an epic kaiju battle. Those are some of the fictional versions of this golden beast, but what does it look like in reality?

Arguably the most impressive feat of King Ghidorah has been to make itself such an important part of pop culture that astronomers took note. The King Ghidorah supercluster is a collection of galaxies located around 6.7 billion light-years from Earth. Covering an area of the sky equivalent to 19 full moons, as seen from our vantage point, this cosmic Kaiju was discovered in late 2022 by Japanese astronomers using data from the Subaru Telescope.

The King Ghidorah supercluster is comprised of at least 19 individual associated galaxy clusters. It stretches out for an incredible 1.3 billion light-years, meaning the entire Milky Way could fit across it around 12,300 times. That makes it the largest supercluster ever discovered.

To put into context just how monstrous the King Ghidorah supercluster is, consider the fact that it has a mass equivalent to 10,000,000,000,000,000 suns, 10 times as massive as the Milky Way's home supercluster, Laniakea. Even Godzilla may think twice before attempting to tussle with that particular King Ghidorah!

See King Ghidorah in action in Godzilla Minus Zero, which is showing in theaters in the US and UK from November 6. You can see the preceding movie, Godzilla Minus One, on Netflix.

#842. ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players

Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

“I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”

For many years, says the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa launched its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

“I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” says Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

“Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”

Up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she says. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

“There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour says. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”

Some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

When Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle United, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she says. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”

Though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she says. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

But for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie says candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”

The other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she says bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a new deal being offered.

Even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data shows that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an important fact.

#841. Kaylee Hottle’s Sister Will Finish the Godzilla Actress' Final Role

After Godzilla star Kaylee Hottle died in a car accident earlier this year, it’s been confirmed her older sister Jasmine Hottle will complete the late 18-year-old's final film, What Doesn't Kill Us.

Jasmine Hottle is keeping her sister Kaylee Hottle's memory alive.

After the Godzilla star died in a car accident at age 18 in July, her older sister is stepping in to complete Kaylee's final role in What Doesn't Kill Us, a superhero movie starring actors with real-life disabilities, writer Adam Mingo confirmed.

"Kaylee’s passing was an unimaginable tragedy, and her loss is felt deeply by everyone involved with the project," Mingo told People in an interview published Nov. 11. "When we began discussing how to move forward, the possibility of Jasmine taking on her sister’s role emerged as something particularly meaningful."

And including Jasmine, who like her sister is deaf, was more than a casting replacement, Mingo explained, because of her unique position to "preserve something of Kaylee’s legacy."

Additionally, Jasmine's ability to provide representation to her community was important to the filmmakers. In fact, Jasmine recently graduated as Valedictorian from Texas School for the Deaf, where Kaylee was a senior before she died of blunt-force injuries from the fatal single-vehicle collision in Ijamsville, Maryland, on July 21.

As Mingo put it, Jasmine’s "involvement allows us to honor Kaylee’s memory while continuing the work she was going to be part of," noting the team's commitment to "authentic disability representation, both in front of and behind the camera."

The forthcoming film will follow a group of friends who use their disabilities to follow their dream of becoming superheroes.

As such, the creative team and costars—including Marvel actress Alaqua Cox—are excited to share a story Kaylee would be proud of.

"We believe audiences are ready for a different kind of superhero story," Mingo remarked, "one in which disability isn’t something to be overcome or erased, but an essential part of what makes these characters extraordinary."

Before Kaylee's death, the young star was building a promising career thanks to films like 2021's Godzilla vs. Kong and 2024's Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire alongside Rebecca Hall and Millie Bobby Brown.

Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation at Venus, but it persevered for nine years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express.

Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years.

During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole. It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes. Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras. These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere.

Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this. It performed well, but eventually it stopped listening to commands. The spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere in January 2015.

Venus Express established ESA as the third world organization to successfully send a probe to study Venus, following the United States and Soviet Union. (Japan's JAXA became the fourth five years later.)

"By studying Venus, scientists learn how Earth-like planets change over time," reads a summary of the planet's exploration prepared by The Planetary Society. "Orbital studies [like Venus Express] hint that Venus may have hosted habitable oceans before becoming inhospitable."

"By studying Venus, we can learn how Earth-like planets evolve and what shapes planets throughout the galaxy into temperate, lush worlds instead of sweltering hothouses. Venus also helps scientists model Earth’s climate, and may serve as a cautionary tale on how dramatically a planet’s climate can change," wrote the Society.

ESA returned to Venus in 2018 when BepiColombo, its joint mission with JAXA, used the planet's gravity to redirect its path toward the planet Mercury.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#838. Crystal Palace sack Pierre Sage and in advanced talks to appoint Thomas Frank

Sage goes after 16 games with club bottom of table

He is the favourite to take over at former club Lens

Pierre Sage has been sacked as Crystal Palace’s manager after 16 games, with Thomas Frank in advanced talks to succeed him.

The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June to replace Oliver Glasner, has gone after Sunday’s 3-1 defeat by Liverpool left his team bottom of the Premier League. Frank, out of work since his dismissal by Spurs in February, has emerged as the main candidate to succeed Sage. He spoke to Palace in the summer and is keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford. It is hoped that he will take charge before next Saturday’s trip to Coventry.

The decision to sack Sage was made on Sunday evening but negotiations over compensation for the rest of his three-year contract delayed his exit. A further complication was that Sage has emerged as the favourite to take over at his previous club, Lens, after they sacked Yannick Cahuzac on Tuesday. The Lens owner and president, Joseph Oughourlian, has remained in close contact with Sage and is understood to have held talks about a return. That would mean Palace could avoid paying some compensation to Sage, having spent more than £4m to buy him out of his contract when he replaced Oliver Glasner in the summer.

Palace, who confirmed that Sage’s backroom staff would also depart, said in a statement: “The club would like to place on record its thanks to Pierre and his staff for their efforts during their time in south London, and wish them well for the future. An update on the process of appointing a new manager will be provided in due course.”

Sunday’s defeat was Palace’s fifth in an eight-match run that also included a painful 5-0 hammering by their arch-rivals Brighton. Their only victory in the sequence came in the Carabao Cup at Fulham and they have lost four league fixtures in a row.

Palace have seven points from 10 games, their league victories having come against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, and have conceded the most goals in the division: 24. They have been juggling domestic matches with the Europa League, where they sit 21st in the 36-team table.

Sage signed a three-year contract after leaving Lens, where he won the Coupe de France and qualified for the Champions League in his final season.

Alternatives to Frank include the former Nottingham Forest manager Sean Dyche, who also has his backers at Palace, and Vítor Pereira, another former Forest manager.

Palace have lost their two main central defenders this year, Marc Guéhi moving to Manchester City in January and Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea in the summer. Two loan players – Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor – were signed as replacements. Palace did not land one of Sage’s top targets, the winger Malick Fofana.

Sage is understood to have fallen out with the board over their failure to sign what he regarded as adequate replacements for Guéhi and Lacroix. The Palace chair, Steve Parish, was unhappy with Sage’s treatment of Jaydee Canvot, another centre-back, after the France Under-21 international was dropped from the squad for September’s home defeat by Ipswich, and expressed displeasure after Adam Wharton was substituted in that match.

#837. Frankie Muniz Hospitalized After Crash at Daytona Speedway

Frankie Muniz was hospitalized in Florida on Nov. 11 after he was involved in a crash at the Daytona International Speedway while preparing for the Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic.

Frankie Muniz is navigating a scary situation.

The Malcolm in the Middle star was hospitalized in Florida Nov. 11 as he was in the midst of practicing for the Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic at the Daytona International Speedway.

“Frankie Muniz was involved in an incident while practicing for today’s Proud to Honor event at Daytona International Speedway,” his racing group Team Reaume told E! News in a statement. “He was taken to a local medical facility for further evaluation and is awake and alert.”

E! News has reached out to Muniz’s manager but has not received further comment.

Muniz’s crash occurred as the 40-year-old prepared to drive for Team Air Force during the Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic, which features Ford competitors honoring the six military branches and is set to air on USA Network at 8 p.m. ET and streaming on Fandango.

And while the Agent Cody Banks star hasn’t said goodbye to his acting career for good, he has been keeping his focus on racing after announcing in 2023 that he was following his passion for the sport.

"Ever since childhood, it's been my dream to pursue racing in NASCAR," he shared in a statement at the time. "I look forward to not only demonstrating my ability on the track and just how serious I am in progressing in my racing career, but also showing my son and family what it is to chase your dreams and re-invent yourself."

Muniz—who shares son Mauz, 5, with estranged wife Paige Price—took part in his first professional race on Feb. 18, 2023, which was coincidentally 22 years to the day after the death of Dale Earnhardt during a race that Muniz himself was present for.

He later recalled the racing advice Earnhardt gave him that tragic day.

“He told me, ‘Enjoy it, enjoy the run, because you never know when it’s gonna end,’” Muniz remembered in the 2026 FS1 documentary We’ve Lost Dale Earnhardt: 25 Years Later. “Maybe I talked to him for a total of three minutes. A very impactful three minutes. Especially where my life ended up going.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Starlog" was one of the greatest sci-fi and fantasy magazines ever, and after a 17-year absence, it's being resurrected.

The legendary sci-fi mag went dark back in 2009 as part of the wave of popular publications folding due to years of declining readership and subscriptions. But as of Nov. 13, this geek favorite periodical returns as an annual print edition, and it's available for pre-order now.

It’s another indication of digital fatigue in the world, and fans of a certain age will recall the pleasure of poring over each colorful issue packed with in-depth interviews, behind-the-scenes photos, TV guides, classic movie retrospectives, book reviews, con news, and VFX features.

"Starlog" launched in 1976, in the pre-"Star Wars" days, under the leadership of editor-in-chief Kerry O’Quinn. It first arrived with artist Jack Thurston's beautiful painted "Star Trek" cover, featuring William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk and Leonard Nimoy’s Spock, set against the U.S.S. Enterprise near a shimmering black hole.

The magazine continued to inform the science fiction community about upcoming sci-fi TV shows and blockbuster Hollywood films for over three decades; I fondly recall reading each informative and entertaining monthly issue cover-to-cover.

Just in time to honor its 50th anniversary this year, "Starlog" blasts back into the sci-fi universe with Issue #375 showcasing cover artwork created by Armenian artist Gabriel Yeganyan. Its geek culture legacy, covering iconic franchises like "Star Wars," "Star Trek," and "Alien," will now live on thanks to Fangoria Holdings and io9 co-founder Annalee Newitz, editor-in-chief.

"During its original 33-year run, 'Starlog' documented science fiction as it evolved across film, television, books, technology, and culture," said 'Fangoria's Tara Ansley.

"Fifty years after the magazine first launched, the line between science fiction and the real world has become increasingly difficult to separate. That makes this an especially interesting time to bring 'Starlog' back. Technology may change, but the most compelling questions have always been about people: how we live, what we create, and what kind of future we want to build."

"Starlog" reloads for its first annual edition after a long hiatus on Nov. 13. You can pre-order the first issue (Issue 375 in continuity) on the Starlog website.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. #833. Carrick sacked by Manchester United with team in Premier League relegation zone – live

⚽️ Head coach departs after one win in 11 games ⚽️ Carrick was latest fall guy for dysfunctional hierarchy ⚽️ Have any thoughts? Email John

Michael Carrick has been dismissed by Manchester United. He departs after a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford last Sunday that left the team in the Premier League’s bottom three. United twice fought back from two goals down for a late point against Villa, after a dramatic recovery to defeat Roma in the Champions League five days earlier, but that wasn’t enough.

United are third-bottom in the Premier League, a point behind 17th-placed Coventry, and 17th in the Champions League league phase table. His departure follows a review led by the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and a recommendation to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy.

David Flynn gets in touch: “Hi John, I must say I don’t fully agree that United keep appointing yesterday’s men, they’ve also tried appointing tomorrow’s men (Amorin, Ten Haag) and nobody’s men (Carrick, Ole). It’s actually a broad spectrum of mistakes that they keep making.”

Ben Monroe-Lake gets in touch: “We live in an age of incredibly powerful individuals, people who wield vast amounts of money and influence and increasingly make little attempt to hide how readily they are to fling such influence and money around for their own benefit. Trump, Musk, Huang, Zuckerberg etc.

“And yet at the same time, these people seem entirely unable to not show everyone their arse, on ever more impressive stages, in ever more shocking ways. So the mind trust at Manchester United are a particularly great microcosm of this. Men of a particular age, who voluntarily took up this position, wrested control of the football operations in fact, as they thought they could do it better. Yet it’s obvious how bad they are at this, even without seeing inside their Monaco based boardrooms.

“Extend Ten Hag’s contract based on the performance in one game. Force in a young manager with a rigid tactical plan without the players to support it. Fire the person you paid Newcastle Utd a huge fee to hire, because he points out this is stupid. Keep on the interim manager with little experience and don’t fill the most gaping holes in his squad.

“In between this, fire the tea ladies, make some questionable pronouncements and who can even remember all the gaffes.

“Of course it’s slightly terrifying that people who are essentially “in charge” are so stupid but it’s a little bit mollifying that people that seem happy to wade waist deep into all aspects of our lives are as dumb as I am. All that really separates me from them is luck and being more willing to get up at five in the morning. So perhaps one day someone not a total bozo will make enough money to buy a football club.”

David Wall gets in touch: “One thing that concerns me about Pochettino is how he will engage with the academy. There was a lot made when he was at Spurs about how he favoured young players. But in fact most of those young players were bought in from outside of the club. It was only Kane from their academy who became a regular in the first team (perhaps with Winks, although more as a squad player rather than first choice). Is Pochettino the type of manager who will spend his midweek evenings going to watch the youth sides play, or is he just going to give an instruction about age-profile to the recruitment department?”

Winks started the 2019 Champions League final, as did Kane, rather unfortunately. At Chelsea, there was definite friction with the club hierarchy, though the signs at United are that he could have the personality to create his own powerbase. Within United, there is a great big vacuum that someone needs to fill.

The problem with Pochettino is that he’s very much the face of 2015 rather than 2026, setting aside what was a decent enough USMNT World Cup until it all went wrong. United keep doing this. Louis van Gaal would have been a fine appointment in 1996 rather than 2015, and Jose Mourinho would have been ideal in 2003, rather than 2016. Of course, United had a good manager in those days but times move on.

Joe Taylor gets in touch: “Spurs fan here. I’m a bit confused by the Pochettino-Spurs revisionism. Sometimes managers don’t get credit for taking players that until that point hasn’t achieved anything and turning them into world beaters (eg. Eriksen, Son) but in this case he doesn’t even get credit for players that didn’t do anything before or after his tenure (eg. Dier, Dele Alli, Dembele, Lamela). I’d suggest he had quite a large hand in that squad that supposedly made his life easy. I think he’s perfect for United right now.”

I’d agree. He made the most of what he had, and a player of a couple of players who have achieved very little without his help. There’s a few projects to work on at United.

Warning: Poch may not be an instant cure for the Manchester United malaise.

At Chelsea, just one win from his first six league games, same at Southampton and Espanyol, while at Tottenham he won two and drew two. At PSG, he won four of his first six games, which at that club is probably below par.

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) earlier issued a statement following Carrick’s dismissal pinning the blame for poor results firmly on the ownership. In full below:

double quotation markMichael Carrick’s departure marks another depressing moment for Manchester United. We thank him for his service and for restoring hope during the second half of last season. His standing among supporters remains undiminished.

The reason Manchester United fans have continued to support Michael Carrick in recent weeks is that they know that responsibility for United’s problems do not primarily rest with him or indeed his predecessors as manager.

The Glazers’ debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club. When INEOS came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.

It is time for the owners to explain themselves and show some accountability.

But the discontent at United is not just about matters on the pitch. Far from it.

Aggressive ticketing policies have further damaged relations with supporters. Treating loyal fans principally as a source of revenue undermines their identity and the bond with the team that sustains support through difficult times. Supporters are being asked to pay the price for the owners’ mismanagement as well as their stadium ambitions through higher charges and diminished rights.

The earlier Stretford End banner declaring “The way you treat us is a disgrace” was a warning. The unprecedented scale of the booing at Old Trafford, alongside public criticism from senior players in recent weeks, now points to a deeper deterioration. These are signs of a club becoming more divided, with the bond between supporters, players and those running Manchester United under increasing strain.

MUST warned publicly in January 2025 that alienating supporters risked a downward spiral of worsening atmosphere, performances and financial outcomes. Our subsequent Telegraph article urged Sir Jim Ratcliffe to break that “doom loop” by bringing supporters with him. Those warnings remain painfully relevant.

The owners must allow senior club management to change direction: show accountability, rebuild trust, listen to supporters and recognise that their loyalty is fundamental to football success. Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.

The pattern is repeated, the problems remain the same. Wrote this a couple of weeks ago.

double quotation markBeyond Busby and Ferguson, each United manager who also served felt the lash of desperation of a falling giant. Each of their defenestrations has featured an infighting that would not have been out of place in ancient Rome. Favouritism, nepotism, self-interest, entitlement, complacency and sentimentality have been the betrayal of a legend, to use the title of Michael Crick’s and David Smith’s “j’accuse” book from 1989. Living with the legend and influence of those two managers leads the list of difficulties.

United fans know such history too well. “You lousy bastards, you let him down,” Brian Kidd told teammates when the bullet came for Wilf McGuinness, Busby’s immediate successor, in December 1970. Busby himself had done the deed. A December 1972 meeting at Selhurst Park with Tommy Docherty as Crystal Palace beat United 5-0 hastened the end for Frank O’Farrell.

And with that I shall hand over to John Brewin for the afternoon session.

An email! “I’m a lifelong Spurs fan and enjoyed having Poch as manager,” writes Alan. “But he did have a squad that made his life pretty easy. By the start of his second season, 2015-16, he could field this side: Lloris; Walker, Alderweireld, Vertonghen, Rose; Eriksen, Dier, Dembele; Dele Alli, Kane, Son. Not sure how many of the current United squad would get into that team. Sadly most of them would also get into the current Spurs team!”

The timing of Pochettino’s expected arrival will be interesting. The US men’s side have a Concacaf Nations League game against Haiti in Kingston, Jamaica, on Saturday, with the return leg next Wednesday in Cincinnati. Manchester United travel to Anfield in the Premier League four days later.

The nitty gritty of that is surely forming part of the conversations ongoing now. Either way, US Soccer will be quids-in as Jeff Rueter explains here.

double quotation markThe real boon is his release clause, a reported $10m (£7.5m) option that only a Big Club could afford to spring. Had Pochettino left after the World Cup, coach and federation would have parted with nothing more exchanged than a handshake and some pleasantries. Instead, they forged an insurance policy to make up for what could have been if Pochettino had stayed for a full cycle.

A few comments from below the line on our news story.

Impossible job and yet he still finished third. This is the weakest squad Utd have had in 40 years. That’s not Michael’s fault. He can walk either his head held high. The fish rots from the head and it’s spread right thru the Utd body. Michael got caught up in it, bloody useless players in the main.

Pochettino flatters to decieve, won nothing at Tottenham, PSG are better under Luis Enrique and USA much of a muchness, it'll be another round of we made mistakes yet again at United inside 18 months. And Carrick was treated appallingly by the hierarchy, Relegation would be just desserts.

Thank you Michael. Your conduct was exemplary. Once it became known that WIlcox leads a review, it was clear he would recommend Ratcliffe to fire Carrick. Otherwise he would be to blamed himself. How come the club that was 3rd last year is 3rd from bottom this year, with the same coach? The obvious answer is that recruitment failed. Wilcox can't have that, so better blame coach. I think one of the problems of United and hierarchy is that they are opportunistic in their managerial appointments. Not only they don't have a long-term strategy, they don't even have a short-term strategy and fire coaches when other options they identify previously become available. They fired van Gaal because they contacted Mourinho, they pursued Amorim, now they fire Carrick when they are able to get a deal with Pochettino.

Do yourself a favour and read Barney Ronay’s piece on Poch’s imminent arrival. These lines feel particularly apt:

double quotation markHow do you solve a club that has won two major trophies in 10 years of steady downward progress? Easy. You hire a coach who has also won two major trophies in 13 years of steady downward progress. How do we get back to the dimly remembered recent past? We hire the dimly remembered recent past.

Does this feel like a magic bullet? At this stage hiring Pochettino is like booking the bloke who did Gangnam Style to play the Super Bowl. Yeah, huge fan. Remind me. Weren’t you quite big in 2013?

What next for Michael Carrick is also an interesting question. Has he done enough to put himself in contention for the next Premier League vacancy that comes up? Or is it back to the Championship, where his tenure with Middlesbrough was mixed to say the least? With Regis Le Bris and Matthias Jaissle probably looking the least secure in the top flight at the moment, might a return to the north east be on the cards at some point for the Wallsend-born man? Doesn’t feel quite right, does it? But you never know.

Hello all. Perhaps the most immediate problem facing Mauricio Pochettino when he arrives will be playing personnel. It’s painfully obvious – and is has been for years – that where once Manchester United was home for the best of the best, these days it’s … not. Everyone has their own view on players but when you look at the teamsheets for the key recent games against Aston Villa, Chelsea and, yes, Bournemouth you’d be hard-pressed to suggest that United had a truly superior 20-man matchday squad for those games. And Pochettino isn’t going to be able to fix that overnight.

John Ashdown is here to take the blogging reins.

You have to credit Manchester United. Your local rivals have turned the Premier League into an almost meaningless farce. We are questioning the validity of anything we’ve seen over the past 20 years; wondering how many goals Erling Haaland will get in the Championship. We are looking at the league table from second position down and wishing we’d invested in inflatable bananas a month ago.

And yet here comes the Old Trafford machine: from players to the captain to the manager to the director of football, to the director of the director of football, to a minority owner who feels the UK is being “colonised by immigrants”, to debt-leveraging majority owners who take vast sums out of the club and are collectively saying hold my Ineos-sponsored high-performance wellness immune boost smoothie.

Yes, it’s time to dust down the Manchester United bin-fire article. Read this and compare and contrast. From 11 August 2022: “Reds rinse and repeat: will we ever break the Manchester United crisis cycle?” There are others.

“Yes, it’s time to dust down the Manchester United bin-fire article,” as Max Rushden wrote recently. Another piece that’s well worth revisiting …

Here’s a data graphic on how Manchester United, under Carrick, went from good last season to bad this season.

“Michael Carrick has been at the helm during the Red Devils’ first dip into the relegation zone since 1986 yet somehow is also definitely not at fault. In January 2014 the 13th series of Celebrity Big Brother aired in the UK, the show so popular that its run time was extended by five days before a public vote anointed Jim Davidson the winner. Then, two years later when Brexit happened, people wondered where their tolerant country had gone, lamenting the ephemeral spirit of London 2012 as though the 2011 riots were some kind of fever dream, not a desperate response to decades of structural and institutional racism exacerbated by the cruelty of unnecessary austerity.

The truth is that if security is quickly upended, it was built on quicksand to begin with. Which brings us to Manchester United, easing effortlessly from an uplifting third-place finish to some of the worst football in their history.

It is entirely possible that Alex Ferguson made a deal with the devil to the effect that United would be great until he retired and hilariously dreadful thereafter. But assuming not, his l’état, c’est moi mentality was busy setting up the post-him fall even at the height of the success – itself a consequence of what had gone before.

Pierre Sage has been sacked as Crystal Palace’s manager after 16 games. The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June to replace Oliver Glasner, has gone after Sunday’s 3-1 defeat by Liverpool left his team bottom of the Premier League.

Thomas Frank, out of work since his dismissal by Spurs in February, has emerged as the main candidate to succeed Sage. He spoke to Palace in the summer and is said to be keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford.

“Sadness it’s come to this … more sadness because it’s Michael,” Gary Neville tells Sky Sports News. “I wish he hadn’t got the job at the end of the season … I didn’t expect it to happen this quickly, but it is what it is … the position in the league is terrible [but] the club is spinning on a roundabout again.

“[European] Super League was the ultimate low, a betrayal of the English game … I think this is a low, but you don’t even get angry anymore … you just feel, like, nothing … it makes you numb, I think the fans are sick of it, I think everyone is sick of it.”

“I have been a supporter for 60 years,” emails Graham. “I hope we get relegated, lose lots of money and get rid of the owners. Only in this way will we ever get back to being a club that supporters are truly connected with and are proud of.”

“Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? “In my 53 years supporting United this is most depressing time. Worse, even, than the pre-Fergie years,” emails Robert.

“I disagree with the earlier comment that Carrick is not to blame in some way,” emails Ryan.

After Nottingham Forest 3-1 Manchester City, meanwhile, will Pochettino be appointing a second-ball coach?

Personally I don’t think it would be a bad idea:

As Mauricio Pochettino left the podium to close his final press conference of the last international window, he offered an ambiguous farewell.

“See you next …” Pochettino began as he headed to the tunnels of Allianz Field in Saint Paul, before cutting his sentence short. Then, a bit of a sing-song: “See you next, see you next.”

You don’t need an AI clanker’s autocomplete function to try closing the sentence. “See you next month” would have been synonymous with “see you next window”, after all. Jamie Jackson exclusively revealed on Monday night that Manchester United were about to press the “Sack Carrick” button:

“And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager. Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Gary Neville has called Manchester United “classless” over their actions in the days before Carrick’s sacking.

The manager’s departure was announced on Thursday and Mauricio Pochettino has been lined up to replace him.

Confirmation of Carrick’s sacking came after a period of limbo for the former midfielder, who reported to Carrington on Thursday after taking training on Tuesday and Wednesday.

His fate was sealed the day after a meeting in Monaco, when director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada travelled to see co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Speaking on the Overlap’s Stick to Football podcast, recorded prior to Thursday’s confirmation, Neville said the process feels “clumsy”.

Welcome, Mauricio, to the meat grinder. Or rather, welcome back. We’ve been expecting you. There is nothing surprising in the news Manchester United may be on the verge of appointing Mauricio Pochettino. United are always on the verge of appointing Pochettino. This is a club that has spent 13 years hiring and firing the same structurally doomed manager – same shellshocked eyes, same irresolvable macro-problems – and the last eight years almost but not quite doing this to Pochettino.

Manchester United’s next fixture is the small matter of a Premier League match against Liverpool at Anfield, Sunday 22 November: kick-off 4.30pm.

On Saturday, 28 November, it’s a 3pm kick-off against Brentford in the Premier League.

“After going through the Moyes season,” writes Hugh, “the dross football of Mourinho and Van Gaal, the moments-years of Solskjaer, the Rangnick surgery that never was, the middling Ten Hag, the baffling Amorim, and now a decent man thrust into the meat grinder, this is the first year it’s been genuinely hard to watch Man Utd with any emotion.

“And it’s not because of the football. Clearly, there is sadness and regret within the club that Carrick has been dismissed. But the run of one win in 10 Premier League games was seen as unacceptable “by any measure” – and there is a belief that a different manager will get more from the squad. Performances and results in the last three games – the 2-0 defeat by Chelsea, a stirring 3-2 win against Roma and the 4-4 draw with Villa – were not enough to convince the club hierarchy that they were on the right path.

“As a United fan who was around for the early 90s and the many successes that followed, seeing Carrick go is a sad end to a horrible situation,” emails Chris. “He was the only likeable thing about a club and set of players who I find it harder to support as I get older.

“The fans - and I mean the locals, the ones who go to games, who can remember the days before Ronaldo - we deserve better ... better owners, better attitudes, better standards. Nothing will change with the setup of the club today and we are in this macabre holding pattern of failure, hope, anger and disappointment.

“It’s harder and harder to find the hope that should accompany the appointment of a new manager but what other choice do we have?”

Barney Ronay, there, writing a few days ago.

Here is the statement from the club now published on the official website:

“Manchester United can confirm that Michael Carrick has departed his role as men’s first-team head coach.

“Michael rejoined the club in January and guided the team to a third-placed Premier League finish by winning 12 out of the remaining 17 games of the 2025/26 season, accumulating the highest points tally in the league during that period.

“The club intends to appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible.”

Manchester United have sacked Michael Carrick as their head coach with the team in the Premier League’s relegation zone and lined up Mauricio Pochettino to take over.

Pochettino has a framework agreement to join a club who have one win from their past 11 matches. The USA head coach, a Premier League manager with Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea, has a release clause of about $10m (£7.5m). United will have to pay more to take his staff.

#832. DWTS’ Connor Wood Responds to Fans Wanting Him to Date Rylee Arnold

Dancing With the Stars' Connor Wood had a candid reaction when pro dancer Ezra Sosa suggested that fans were "shipping" him and dance partner Rylee Arnold to date.

Dancing With the Stars' Connor Wood is quickstepping past chatter about his friendship with dance partner Rylee Arnold.

In fact, the comedian also known as Fibula had a hilarious response when DWTS pro Ezra Sosa pressed him about fans "shipping" the pair to take their chemistry off the dance floor and date in real life.

"What do you say?" Sosa teased on a TikTok Live during the ABC dance competition series' Nov. 10 broadcast, prompting Wood to briefly stumble on his words before quipping, "I say, 'Thank you for watching.'"

Besides, Wood has made it clear about his actual celeb crush. After all, the 31-year-old was kicking himself when he recently found out that he had once unintentionally snubbed Jennifer Lawrence.

“I saw you on 8th avenue drinking a smoothie and you paid me no mind,” Lawrence commented on one of Wood's social media videos, prompting him to pretend to choke himself in an Oct. 21 TikTok before adding, "This is rolling around in my head.”

As for where Arnold stands with Wood? The 21-year-old—who's been dating college football star Walker Lyon since 2024—considers the two to be great friends.

“It just feels natural,” Arnold told Entertainment Weekly in last month. “I think naturally we just have so much fun together. We feel comfortable with each other.”

Wood agreed, adding that "it was an act of God that we were paired together."

“We don’t really have any missed connects," he continued. "We have this connection that isn’t really faulted by like, ‘Oh, I can’t get this step,’ or ‘I can’t do this move.’”

And though their close bond has left many fans head over heels, Arnold has assured that it's "just dancing."

“I’ve grown up being close to a man’s face since I was 10 years old. Honestly, it’s just second nature," she told TV Insider in September. "To have that chemistry helps you get through the dance, get through the steps."

But while Wood and Arnold's partnership is strictly platonic, read on for DWTS couples who tangoed into a romance.

The season 33 partners dated for about seven months between 2024 and spring 2025.

In April 2025, the fellow DWTS pros kissed on the lips onstage on the final night of the series' 2025 tour during their show-closing duet dance, confirming months of romance rumors.

Months after placing fifth in the 31st season of the dance show, the couple confirmed their romance on Valentine's Day 2023. "My Valentine," the CODA actor captioned a selfie with the choreographer. "Happy Valentine's Day!"

Stewart and Durant then announced their engagement in December 2023 and married in front of a trouple of DWTS pros in August 2025.

While she was partnered with Hayes Grier, the two hit it off during season 21's Switch Up Week, with Skarlatos calling the pro dancer "so hot." After her elimination, Slater teased that they two had yet to go on a date, saying, "We'll see."

Meanwhile, Skarlatos playfully told E! News, "No comment!"

The dance pro and Bachelorette alum were romantically linked while competing together on DWTS' season 33 in 2024. However, their offscreen chemistry fizzled out by June 2025 shortly after Tran returned to Miami to finish her master's degree.

Which bring us to these two. After dating a little on-and-off since 2011, the pros got engaged live on the show in October 2016 and were married in March 2018. However, E! News confirmed in August 2022 that Slater and Farber were going their separate ways after four years of marriage.

"It's not a nightmare at all," Slater told E! News. "We support each other so much that I want the very best for Sasha. We support each other, very, very truly."

Chmerkovskiy and Johnson were dating in 2015, before she was promoted to pro dancer. They got engaged in June of 2018 before making it official and walking down the aisle in April of 2019. The two welcomed son Rome Valentin in January 2023.

"Life is awesome," Chmerkovskiy told E! News in May 2023. Becoming a dad "definitely elevated my joy for life, my joy for my family, and every day I learn something new being a father."

In December 2020, E! News learned the Selling Sunset star was dating the Dancing With the Stars pro after they had competed separately on season 29.

However, after two months of dating, E! News exclusively confirmed they had called it quits. At the time, a source close to the realtor said, "They had a fun time together but in the end, decided it would be best if they part ways. They are still friendly and cordial. It wasn't a messy breakup, just wasn't the right fit or right timing."

Platonic throughout their seventh-place-finishing 2017 run, the Total Bellas star and the former Dancing With the Stars pro found their way back to each other after her split from John Cena in 2018. Garcia confirmed her relationship with Chigvintsev in May 2019, and they got engaged later that year.

The WWE Hall of Famer learned she was expecting soon after their Paris engagement, with them welcoming son Matteo Artemovich Chigvintsev in 2020.

Sadly, though, the pair are no longer partnering up. Garcia filed for divorce in September 2024, two weeks after Chigvintsev was arrested on suspicion of domestic violence. Ultimately, the Napa County District Attorney's office announced they decided not to file charges against him "after a thorough review of the criminal investigation and careful evaluation of the evidence presented to the DA’s Office."

The pair settled their divorce in November 2024, with Garcia's rep noting the two also dropped their "the domestic violence restraining orders against each other in an effort to move on with their lives and effectively co-parent their son."

The model and the relatively new pro flirted up a storm throughout season 27, and Ren had admitted on the show that she had a crush on him. At the time, a source even told E! News that they "really enjoy each other's company" and were "seeing where things go."

However, multiple outlets reported in December 2018 that the pair had split.

The professional dancers got engaged on Dec. 5, 2015, after dating since 2012. Maks proposed onstage at the SWAY: A Dance Trilogy event in Miami. Six months after welcoming their son Shai, the lovebirds exchanged vows during a lavish ceremony in July 2017. They then welcomed baby Rio in June 2023 and their third son Milan in July 2024.

The partners struck up a romance in season five, but broke up a few months after their shocking exit. Still, Bryan and Ballas remained friendly, with The Cheetah Girls star even returning to the ballroom to cheer for him the following season.

Funnily enough, the duo had gone out on several dates before he even signed up for the show. And while they denied any romance rumors during season 18, that didn't stop them from playing up their chemistry during performances.

Soon after the Shark Tank star announced he was separating from his wife of 14 years Diane Plese, sources confirmed to E! News that he and Kym Johnson, his pro partner from season 20, were dating and "really happy together."

While Robert and Kym at first played coy about the nature of their relationship, that quickly stopped. They were engaged in February 2016, married by June 2016, and welcomed twins in April 2018.

Married since 2014, the pros announced the arrival of their daughter Nikita in May 2023.

Daniella shared the happy news by posting a photo and video of Pasha with Nikita to Instagram Stories. She wrote "daddy's girl" alongside the clip and "My Geminis" beside the picture.

After showing off their insane chemistry during the sixth season, the duo dated for nearly a year before announcing their 2009 breakup in the most cordial way ever: matching tweets!
