#815. A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests

Something unusual is happening inside the enormous atmosphere of Betelgeuse, one of the most recognizable stars in the night sky. Astronomers have detected subtle changes in the star's shape that suggest something is moving through its outer layers, disturbing the surrounding gas like an unseen visitor making noise inside a house. (Metaphorically speaking.) New observations point to a likely culprit: Siwarha, a recently discovered companion star that appears to be traveling through Betelgeuse's atmosphere.

Betelgeuse is a massive red supergiant located in the constellation Orion, where it forms the famous hunter's shoulder. Although the star has fascinated astronomers for generations, it attracted worldwide attention in late 2019 and early 2020 when its brightness unexpectedly plunged to its lowest recorded level in more than 100 years. The event, known as the Great Dimming, raised questions about what was happening inside the aging star.

Now, observations from the U.S. National Science Foundation's Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) reveal that Betelgeuse's vast outer atmosphere has largely returned to normal. More intriguingly, the measurements provide new evidence that a nearby companion star is physically disturbing the giant star's atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, working with scientists from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team analyzed observations gathered between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 GHz to 485 GHz.

Different radio frequencies allow astronomers to examine different depths within a star's atmosphere. By combining the observations from both telescopes, the researchers reconstructed the structure of Betelgeuse's outer layers, beginning just above its visible surface and extending outward to several times its radius.

"It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here," said Matthews. "The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing."

Betelgeuse Recovers From Its Mysterious Great Dimming

The latest measurements also help scientists understand how Betelgeuse has changed since its extraordinary fading episode. Several months before the Great Dimming (when Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of solar material, partially blocking our view), an earlier investigation led by Matthews detected unusually low temperatures in the star's atmosphere at radio wavelengths.

At the time, researchers suggested that turbulent convection deep inside Betelgeuse may have generated a shock wave that traveled outward and disrupted the surrounding gas. That disturbance could have helped trigger the enormous release of material that later formed dust and obscured part of the star's light.

The new observations indicate that the atmosphere has since warmed to temperatures more typical of Betelgeuse. At a distance of approximately 2.7 times the star's radius, the gas now has a measured brightness temperature of about 3,500 Kelvin (comparable to Betelgeuse's own surface temperature).

Astronomers Discover an Unexpectedly Cold Atmospheric Layer

The researchers also confirmed a feature that scientists had suspected existed for years: a region of unusually cool gas between Betelgeuse's visible surface and its higher atmospheric layer, known as the chromosphere.

Using ALMA at its highest observed frequencies, the team was able to probe closer to the star's surface than previous radio measurements had allowed. The results revealed temperatures falling to approximately 2,200 Kelvin, more than 1,000 degrees below the temperature of the visible surface, or photosphere.

This cool region corresponds to the "MOLsphere," a layer containing molecular gas that astronomers had previously identified primarily through infrared observations. The new radio measurements provide a much more direct examination of this elusive part of Betelgeuse's atmosphere and confirm the long-suspected "temperature minimum."

A Hidden Companion Star May Be Distorting Betelgeuse

One of the most intriguing discoveries involves Siwarha, the smaller star believed to orbit extremely close to Betelgeuse. Astronomers first proposed the companion's existence in 2024 as a possible explanation for a puzzling cycle in which Betelgeuse's brightness changes approximately every 2,100 days. Subsequent direct imaging and spectroscopic observations have provided additional support for the companion's existence.

The name Siwarha reflects its relationship with Betelgeuse. The giant star's name comes from the Arabic expression meaning "the hand of al-Jawza," while Siwarha means "her bracelet."

Unlike a planet or star traveling far from its host, Siwarha is believed to follow an orbit that takes it directly through Betelgeuse's extended atmosphere. Its estimated orbital distance is only about twice the red supergiant's radius.

"This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere," Matthews explained.

As Siwarha moves along its orbit, it may push through the surrounding gas much like a fast boat cutting through water. The resulting wake could disturb the atmosphere, producing changes that astronomers can detect even though the smaller star itself remains invisible in the radio observations.

In fact, the researchers calculated that Siwarha is likely tens to hundreds of times too faint to be detected directly with the radio measurements they collected. Instead, they searched for indirect evidence of its presence by studying the shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere.

Betelgeuse's Changing Shape Reveals New Clues

The scientists discovered that Betelgeuse does not always appear perfectly round at radio wavelengths. Its atmosphere sometimes develops a slightly stretched, oval appearance, and the timing of these changes appears to match the expected position of Siwarha.

To investigate this connection, the team measured the atmosphere's departure from a circular shape ("ellipticity") across observations taken at different times.

They found that Betelgeuse tends to look more elongated when Siwarha is expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from the giant star. When the companion is predicted to pass in front of or behind Betelgeuse from our perspective, the atmosphere appears rounder.

This relationship provides compelling evidence that the smaller star may be influencing the shape of Betelgeuse's outer layers through gravity and its physical passage through the gas.

The effect resembles noticing ripples spreading across a pond without being able to see what caused them. Although Siwarha remains too faint to identify directly at radio wavelengths, the changing shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere may reveal its movement around the larger star.

Future Observations Could Reveal More About Betelgeuse

Despite the promising results, astronomers emphasize that additional observations are necessary to confirm the connection between Siwarha's orbit and the atmospheric distortions. Measurements covering more of the companion's orbital cycle, particularly at radio frequencies that have not yet been studied extensively, could help establish how strongly the smaller star affects Betelgeuse.

More advanced instruments may eventually provide an even clearer picture. The Next Generation Very Large Array, an observatory currently under development, is expected to make detailed studies of nearby stars and their atmospheres much easier.

Such observations could reveal not only how companion stars influence their massive neighbors, but also how aging red supergiants lose material as they approach the final stages of their lives. Understanding these interactions may help astronomers better explain the complicated processes that shape the evolution of enormous stars like Betelgeuse.

The findings were published in The Astronomical Journal in a paper titled "New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion."

The future of flight meets space exploration as a futuristic electric aircraft hovers beside Blue Origin's massive New Glenn rocket stage.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A futuristic single-person aircraft takes to the skies at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, with the upper stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket providing a dramatic backdrop.

The unusual scene was captured during the MAX POWER event, which brought together innovators and emerging technologies at the iconic spaceflight facility.

The photograph shows a single-person electric aircraft called Jetson ONE, developed by Jetson, a US-based company working to bring personal flight to the skies.

The compact rotorcraft uses multiple propellers to climb into the air, allowing it to take off and vertically without the need for a runway.

The aircraft was performing flight demonstrations during the UP.Summit gathering, which formed part of the larger MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center.

During the demonstrations, the Jetson ONE demonstrated its ability to maneuver through the air and hover in place, giving spectators a close-up look at the technology in action.

The photograph offers a fascinating glimpse at two very different approaches to flight. While Jetson is developing small electric aircraft designed for personal transportation, Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket is built to carry payloads far beyond Earth's atmosphere.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#810. Steph Curry Defends Wife Ayesha Curry From Criticism Over Movie Kiss

NBA power couple Steph and Ayesha Curry defended their marriage from criticism of her sharing romantic moments onscreen with costar Matthew Daddario in a Christmas movie.

Steph Curry doesn't think Ayesha Curry dropped the ball.

As a clip of Ayesha's onscreen kiss in Second Chance Christmas drew criticism online because of her real-life role as Steph's wife—including from several ballers in the professional sports world—the Golden State Warrior stepped in to shut down the "noise."

"You're trying to step on the accomplishments of my wife, and obviously leading podcast tapings and topics, and giving opinions on somebody else's wife," Steph explained on Instagram Nov. 11, calling out anybody "who feels the need to want to have to jump in and give an opinion on something you don't really know about."

In defending his wife of 15 years, the NBA champion called out Warriors alums Nick Young and Gilbert Arenas for referring to Ayesha as a "blemish" compared to other famous WAGs, like LeBron James' wife Savannah James, on their We Said What We Said podcast Nov 7. Steph also referenced retired Philadelphia Eagles Emmanuel Acho and LeSean McCoy, who questioned if Ayesha took the role to get her husband's attention on their podcast, Speakeasy, the week before.

Steph said the negativity "speaks to a bigger conversation on how you view women in this world and what they're allowed and what they're not allowed to do, even the ignorance behind how acting works."

And the 38-year-old's other half was on the same page about the fuss over her scripted embrace with costar Matthew Daddario, as Ayesha wrote on X with a crying emoji, "It's not even real you guys are annoying."

As such, the Bay Area hero advised Ayesha's critics to opt for support instead of judgment in the future, and gave direction on how to nail their next act: apologizing.

"Maybe the apology can be as loud as y'all leading y'all shows with this topic," Steph continued. "Appreciate the free pub."

And after the off-court drilling, some of Ayesha's critics have done exactly that.

"I'm sorry, Steph. You my dog, I love you," Nick admitted on the Gil's Arena podcast following Steph's video. "If I say anything, I apologize like a man."

For his part, Gilbert defended his comments because he said they came from a good place.

“This is exactly why I made the comment, because he’s a professional," Gilbert explained. "He says the right things. If you gotta judge this family, the only blemish is the things that his wife has said."

Still, the podcaster added, "I didn't mean it like that. I was just saying he's such a perfect dude."

For more NBA players who consider their relationship a slam dunk, keep reading...

All Jordyn Woods wanted for Christmas in 2025 was Karl-Anthony Towns' rooftop proposal. "Marry Christmas," the model captioned her Dec. 25 Instagram post, showing the New York Knicks center taking a knee at NYC's Overstory.

And while the massive rectangular sparkler she's been sporting since 2024 was quite the winning play, simply having fun together are the true Xs and Os to their romance. "I think it's kind of cool dating your best friend," she said on her Instagram series Regular-ish in 2021. "We know each other. We know each other's hearts. We know each other on good days and bad days and we've been through a lot of bad days together."

Of course, Aug. 15, 2026 was one of the best yet, the pair marrying in front of their squad in Malibu.

Just because singer Coco Jones wasn't ready to open up her romantic playbook doesn't mean she was hiding her years-long romance with Cleveland Cavaliers shooting guard Donovan Mitchell. "Secrecy is not what I prefer," the "ICU" musician explained during a March 2025 appearance on Club Shay Shay. "I don’t want to feel like I have to be somebody secret. I don’t want to make anybody feel like they’re mine."

Instead, added the Bel-Air actress, "For me, I'm trying to protect myself, and I’m trying to protect my family and who I love, so I am more private."

But the truth is, maybe she, she, she, she, she needs the seven-time NBA All-Star, who shared drone footage of his oceanside proposal in July 2025. Diving into her bridal era, "It's unexplainable," she told E! News at the 2026 Grammys. "I'm like, 'Wow, I've been to so many events, I've planned so many things, I've been to so many fittings, I've worn so many amazing things, but this is unexplainable.'"

Her hard work netted a dream wedding when they wed in Connecticut on Aug. 1, 2026.

At Jayson Tatum's lowest point, it was his family that convinced him to keep shooting his shot. When the Boston Celtics' star forward ruptured his Achilles during the 2025 playoffs, "I could have been like, 'You know what, I'm done. I've accomplished enough,'' the 2024 champ admitted to E! News. "But I thought about the people I would be letting down."

That included sons Deuce (from a previous relationship) and Dylan, with singer girlfriend Ella Mai. "I thought about my kids," the six-time All-Star explained. "Use this opportunity to show them, 'This is what dad went through, and he had a choice to make. We always have choices to make in our lives. What choice are you going to make?'"

One key move that he and the "Boo’d Up" musician decided on is to not diagram their five-plus year relationship. "I think it’s been a weird topic because obviously I never announced it myself," she explained during a December 2025 episode of Capital XTRA. "So, people don’t know whether or not to say it. But I’m not going to act like I don’t have a child. I have a child."

A talented one, at that. "I try not to overdo it because I don’t want him to grow up and be like, 'She just pushed her music down my throat,'" she told E! of their 2024 arrival. "But I do try and play a lot of music around him."

When Philadelphia 76ers big man Joel Embiid was first introduced to future wife Anne de Palma at a 2018 dinner with a mutual friend, he avoided a full-court press. Instead, she told ESPN in 2021, "It started off as a beautiful friendship."

Both transplants to the U.S.—he left Cameroon as a teen to play basketball; the Brazilian model signed her first contract at age 14—they soon learned they each spoke French and shared a love of soccer. "We FaceTimed every day for a while," de Palma continued, but she soon realized he was her personal MVP. "He just has this personality where he wants to motivate you."

Three years after the SI Swimsuit fixture and the seven-time All-Star welcomed son Arthur (named for his younger brother, who died in a 2014 car crash) in September 2020, they wed in the Hamptons. "He pushes all of us to be the best of ourselves," de Palma raved to ESPN of the 76ers center. "That's the type of person you want to have around."

Las Vegas Aces standout A'ja Wilson isn't just an MVP to the WNBA, where she nabbed her league-leading fourth title in 2025. She also provides a crucial lift to boyfriend Bam Adebayo. When the Miami Heat's star center bested Kobe Bryant's record, scoring 83 points against the Washington Wizards on March 10, 2026, he credited his longtime teammate.

"To have 83 the first game she's here is very special," the three-time All-Star said in a video shared by the NBA on social media. "The behind-the-scenes, the workouts, the conversations, they're very motivating, and obviously you see what she does ... you get inspired by that. I'm thankful to have her in my life."

He provides quite the assist as well. When the University of South Carolina retired her jersey in 2025, Wilson shared, "I wouldn't be who I am today without the love, support and sacrifices of so many people. And what a blessing to have those most special to me courtside today, especially my favorite Olympian from out of town."

Still, there have been definitive clues that the Bayou Barbie has found her Ken in Orlando Magic center Wendell Carter Jr. "That’s a sign," the Atlanta Dream power forward captioned a TikTok showcasing an impressive arrangements of roses, "that’s a signnnn." And it was certainly a big play when the Duke alum turned up to the 2025 WNBA All-Star game sporting a t-shirt baring Reese's visage.

The NCAA champ—set to appear on season two of The Hunting Wives—returned the favor, attending a December 2025 Magic game in a jersey emblazoned with the words "My Man."

When it comes to planning her future wedding to Milwaukee Bucks power forward Kyle Kuzma, model Winnie Harlow is still studying that metaphorical game film. "At this point, we're trying to get to a point of where," she explained to E! News in September 2025, seven months after the NBA champ proposed during a Valentine's Day trip to Turks and Caicos, "and then we can get everything flowing."

A few keys to the game: "I'm an island vibe," explained the America's Next Top Model alum. "So, I really want to have warm weather, and I want to have a lot of dancing. I'm that type."

And no doubt Kuzma will dish out some key assists, having truly scored with his island engagement. "I never really asked her what type of ring she liked or anything," he told Vogue of dreaming up the 8.5-carat stunner. "I just wanted to draw a picture of what I felt resembled her—something that was elegant, but very timeless and simplistic at the same time."

Memphis native GloRilla left a Thanksgiving 2024 game between her hometown Grizzlies and the New Orleans Pelicans feeling quite grateful that their star forward Brandon Ingram made a move. "But that's it," the musician told Complex in 2025, "that's all I'm gonna say!"

But every now and then, she'll throw it down. As she wrote in a January 2026 Instagram post, "Might let him dunk dis like he dunk da balllll."

The true MVP of the household, Savannah Brinson was small forward LeBron James' teammate long before he was collecting championships with Dwyane Wade, Kyrie Irving and Anthony Davis. And during that first date to an Akron, Ohio Outback Steakhouse, the cheerleader and softball player had no inkling that the basketball standout from her rival high school would go on to rule the NBA. "I just thought he'd be a hometown hero for his era," she told Harper's Bazaar, "and it would be over."

Fast forward a decade or so, and she and 2003's No. 1 draft pick were married at an event so star-studded Beyoncé and Jay-Z were on hand to perform their hit "Crazy in Love."

After eight seasons in L.A., where James took his trophy-winning talents to the Lakers, he announced plans to finish his career with the Philadelphia 76ers in July 2026.

"The only reason why I can do what I do at the highest level both on and off the floor is my because my best friend got my back regardless the outcome!" he wrote in a November 2019 tribute. "I'm just the car, she's the engine!"

A two-time defensive player of the year, Los Angeles Clippers forward Kawhi Leonard is also skilled at blocking inquiries into his personal life. More than a decade into his romance with fellow San Diego State University alum Kishele Shipley, neither has even confirmed if they've wed. And fans were surprised to learn in April 2019 that the two-time champ (who, like his partner, doesn't have a public Instagram) missed a game because Shipley had given birth to their second child, son Mark Leonard.

"He doesn't give a damn about the stardom," former coach Gregg Popovich has said. Daughter Kaliyah Leonard remains unimpressed as well, the then-4-year-old choosing the Toronto Raptors' victory parade in 2019 as the perfect spot to take a nap!

Hard to believe two-time NBA MVP Steph Curry failed to connect on his initial move with now-wife Ayesha Curry. But when the then-Davidson College standout went in for a kiss during a hang with his former youth group pal, she ducked.

Thankfully, "We had a do-over!" she told told E! News' Jason Kennedy in October 2017. And a few years after that first kiss in his parents' driveway back in their hometown of Charlotte, he proposed in that very spot. "Yeah," he told Parents, "it was like The Notebook."

When they discovered months after their 2011 vows they were expecting their first child—future press conference scene-stealer Riley—Ayesha worried she'd never fully find her professional footing.

But more than a decade, three more kids—daughter Ryan joined the squad in 2015, followed by brothers Canon and Caius in 2018 and 2024—and an entire lifestyle empire later, she's done just fine, her list of titles including cookbook author, Food Network personality, model and philanthropist.

Just don't saddle her with the term "basketball wife." As she shrewdly pointed out to ABC News, "I mean, I don't think my husband would call himself 'chef's wife.'"

We love a man who stays on brand. Back in 2016, Clippers guard Bradley Beal took the beauty entrepreneur "to the top of the Ferris wheel in Vegas, and asked me to be your girlfriend," she shared on Instagram. Four years and two sons—Bradley Jr. and Braylon—he brought her to a similar ride in Maryland. "Now the second time you're on a Ferris wheel, I'm asking you to be my wife," the three-time All-Star said in clip of his January 2020 proposal.

Her answer, of course, was an unequivocal yes. "No one else id rather spend my life with," wrote the XO By Kamiah founder, who welcomed third son Braxton in 2022 ahead of their vows and fourth son Braydie in July 2026. "Thank you for helping me evolve into the woman I've become, and for constantly challenging me to become better each and everyday."

As St. Joe's best offensive player for two consecutive seasons in the mid-2000s, guard Ayahna Cornish-Lowry isn't your typical courtside cheerleader. Sharing with Canadian lifestyle site The Kit in 2019 that she prefers "to be close to the action," the mom of sons Karter Lowry and Kameron Lowry said she doesn't just zero in on her husband Kyle Lowry.

Rather she's taking in every set that his squad runs: "I don't focus in on just Kyle, I try to watch the whole game and the whole team and see what's going on. I love watching it from a basketball eye."

And she's not afraid to give the six-time All-Star and Olympic gold medalist, who announced his retirement in July 2026, her take on how he's running the floor. "He'll come up to me during time-outs, that's how close I am," she said of the point guard, her sweetheart since their days at Philadelphia's Cardinal Dougherty High. "If I see something, I try to mouth it to him. Maybe he'll get it."

Draymond Green, the Warriors' outspoken four-time All-Star isn't exactly known for his subtlety. So when he asked Hazel Renee to be his bride in January 2019, he went full court press. There was a helicopter ride to a yacht filled with their family, friends and kids Olive Jay and Draymond Jamal Green Jr., a six-carat Jason of Beverly Hills diamond and no less than Golden State coach Steve Kerr spilling the news to the press.

After sharing that he and the Empire actress were holding their vows around a planned return trip to the Olympics, COVID-19 forced them to reschedule and focus on a new milestone: Welcoming daughter Cash in October 2020.

"Our journey that we are on has been nothing short of amazing!" he wrote in a 2020 birthday tribute. "Through the good and bad times you continue to be the rock of our family."

Finally walking down the aisle in 2022 (with Vogue publishing photos from their vows), the pair welcomed daughter Hunni in 2023 and their latest arrival in Feburary 2026.

Known for racking up the points, recently retired point guard Russell Westbrook took on the role of cheerleader, hyping up bride Nina Westbrook as she nailed shot after shot in a March 2020 Instagram video. And it's not as if he was blowing hot air. Now a licensed marriage and couples therapist, Nina was once UCLA's fastest players when she spied a flashy young point guard winking at her as he nailed a breakaway dunk. "You were pretty good out there tonight," she reportedly told him after the game. "It's easy to play like that when you have someone to play for," he shot back.

More than a decade later they're juggling their Why Not? children's foundation with raising son Noah and twin daughters Skye and Jordyn and enjoying the occasional dinner-and-a-movie night in. "There is not a thing you won't do to bring a laughter and joy to our children's life," she raved in a Father's Day post. "You are the coolest dad, the definition of fun, and the embodiment of love."

At this point, it's unclear who gets more play in Sports Illustrated—the Utah Jazz big man Kevin Love or Swimsuit Issue cover girl Kate Bock, a fixture since being named Rookie of the Year in 2013. Not that her guy is feeling competitive. "This is a timeless cover," he wrote of the 2020 edition in a congratulatory post. "It could not be a better representation of the beautiful woman you are and continue to be. I'm just so happy for you."

More than a year after the five-time All-Star power forward proposed during a January 2021 birthday celebration, they wed at the New York Public Library.

"We both envisioned an old-school New York City, Great Gatbsy-inspired, black and white ball for the big day," the Love Kate founder detailed to Vogue. "That was the easy part! The hard part was just making the small detailed decisions—whether it was a specific linen, the seating chart, or where to get ready."

Soon after, they were prepping for a new era, the two welcoming daughter James in June 2023 and her younger sister Leighton on Valentine's Day 2025.

You know you're basketball royalty when your wedding party includes LeBron James and his bride. In fact, everyone from Dwyane Wade and Carmelo Anthony (plus Gabrielle Union and LaLa Anthony) to Ludacris and Kevin Hart turned out for Chris Paul and Jada Crawley's 2011 Charlotte vows, with no less than Robin Thicke providing the wedding music.

And while an in-ceremony performance by gospel legend BeBe Winans and some 10,000 roses, orchids and hydrangeas is nice, nothing is more important to the Thunder's 12-time All-Star than his top teammate.

His day one since they met at Wake Forest University, "I truly love Jada; she has been there for the ups and the downs," the recently retired point guard told Essence of the philanthropist, mom to Christopher II and Camryn. "Basketball isn't going to last forever. Jada and I love spending time with each other, genuinely."

In the Horford family, it's Al Horford's bride that truly holds court. Model and singer Amelia Vega's titles include Miss Dominican Republic 2002 and Miss Universe 2003.

Though it took two meetings, the first at the Latin Pride Awards in Boston and the second four years later working together on a campaign for children with cancer, the Dominican born five-time All-Star said he was confident early on that he'd found his forever teammate.

"We started dating and became pretty obvious that she was the right person for me. It just felt right," the Warriors power forward told Latina in 2013. "I would always make fun of people, or wouldn't believe something like that was true. I felt right with her and I knew that I wanted to marry her."

More than a decade in, "Married life is awesome," said the University of Florida standout, dad to Ean, Alía, Ava, Nova and Mila with the Miami boutique owner. "We're building something special—our lives together."

Back in 2008 when Portland Trailblazers guard Jrue Holiday was a stand-out freshman at UCLA, an autograph seeker approached him at a women's basketball game, thinking he was his teammate Darren Collison. Witnessing the whole exchange, Lauren Holiday, a member of the Bruins soccer team, chimed in, "Don't worry, you're cuter than Darren."

It's a decidedly adorable meet-cute, but the rest of their love story is even better. Retired from the national women's team, the World Cup champ and two-time gold medalist was nearly five months pregnant when she learned she had a brain tumor. Without thought, Jrue took a months-long sabbatical from his NBA gig in 2016 to be at his bride's side until the meningioma was successfully removed.

Now a devoted father to theirdaughter Jrue and son Hendricks, "You show us everyday what unconditional love looks like," Lauren wrote in a Father's Day tribute. You show up for us on your best and your worst days and it never feels like you give us any less."

Just a few years removed from his career at Butler University, now-retired forward Gordon Hayward shot his shot, asking recent high school grad Robyn Hayward to be his bride on Christmas Eve 2013. Married the following May, the athletes—she was a standout volleyball player at her Indiana high school—have steadily been putting together their own squad ever since.

Son Theo joined daughters Bernie, Charlie and Nora in September 2020 while Gordon was battling it out in the bubble with the Boston Celtics.

And despite having to play zone with all their little ones, the duo haven't ruled out bringing on more teammates. "Bernie is sweet and gentle, Charlie is always doing things on her own time and beats to her own drum, Nora makes sure Theo knows she's the boss and has no fear at all, and Theo is pretty unbothered and chill (so far)," she detailed in a December 2020 post. "This is what 4 kids 5 and under looks like (for us)... @gordonhayward do you want more kids?"

Turns out he was ready to run another play. The couple welcomed son Sebastian in September 2025.

#809. USA withdraw from U17 World Cup

The USA reached the last 32 of last year's Under-17 World Cup, the first of five successive editions to be held annually in Qatar

The USA have withdrawn from the Under-17 World Cup in Qatar because of the risk of armed conflict.

In a letter sent to players and seen by news agency Reuters, US Soccer said it made the decision "in light of current circumstances".

It cited advice from the US Department of State, which issued a level three travel advisory, external for Qatar last month.

That came a day after Yemen's Houthi movement carried out a deadly attack on an airport in neighbouring Saudi Arabia, while air strikes have continued on Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

The 48-team tournament runs from 19 November to 13 December, and the USA were due to play group games against Montenegro, Chile and Algeria.

The US travel advisory mentioned Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure, and warned that hostilities "have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area".

The update told Americans to reconsider travel to Qatar because of "risk of armed conflict".

"The well-being of our players and staff will always be our top priority," US Soccer said in the letter.

It said it would notify the players' clubs and asked players not to comment publicly until their withdrawal has been announced by tournament organisers Fifa.

The 2027 Asian Cup - Asia's version of the European Championships - was due to take place in Saudi Arabia from 7 January to 5 February, but has been postponed by almost a year because of the conflict.

The wife of England striker Ollie Watkins, who plays in the Saudi Pro League, has taken their children back to the UK until the situation "calms down".

#808. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened

The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached an important milestone in its mission to investigate a historic asteroid collision. For the first time, its onboard camera has captured the two asteroids Didymos and Dimorphos as separate objects rather than a single point of light.

The asteroid pair is currently about 197 million kilometers from Earth. Hera obtained the new image on the evening of October 18 using its black-and-white Asteroid Framing Camera, while the spacecraft was approximately 1,280 kilometers from its targets.

"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," explains Michael Kueppers. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."

The breakthrough image follows a successful series of maneuvers designed to slow Hera as it approaches the asteroid system. Earlier in October, the spacecraft fired its thrusters twice, with one week between the maneuvers. These adjustments reduced its speed relative to the asteroids to just 20 meters per second, allowing mission controllers to carefully manage the remaining approach.

Although the two asteroids appear tiny in the initial image, they are substantial objects. Dimorphos measures about 151 meters across, making it roughly comparable in size to the Great Pyramid of Giza. Its larger companion, Didymos, is approximately 780 meters in diameter, slightly smaller than the height of Dubai's Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building.

Dimorphos travels around Didymos at an average separation of just 1.15 kilometers, moving at a speed of approximately 18 centimeters per second.

"For the very first time we are seeing through Hera's own eyes the very double asteroid system that the mission was designed and built for," adds mission manager Ian Carnelli.

"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer. We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos -- the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action -- on 25 November."

Uncovering the Aftermath of NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision

Hera's arrival will give scientists an opportunity to examine the results of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment conducted four years earlier.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second. The impact blasted debris as far as 10,000 kilometers into space and shortened the asteroid's orbital period around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes.

The experiment demonstrated that a spacecraft could deliberately change an asteroid's motion, an achievement with potentially enormous implications for protecting Earth from future asteroid threats.

However, the collision also produced results that scientists are still trying to fully explain. The asteroid's orbital change was substantially greater than computer simulations had predicted, raising questions about its physical properties and how it responded to the impact.

Researchers still do not know whether DART left a crater on Dimorphos or significantly altered the asteroid's overall shape. They also need more precise measurements of its composition, internal structure, and mass to understand why the collision was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential for transforming the 'kinetic impact' approach into a reliable planetary defense strategy.

Hera Prepares for a Detailed Asteroid Investigation

Over the coming months, Hera will carry out a detailed 'crash site investigation' to uncover what NASA's collision actually did to Dimorphos.

The spacecraft will use a collection of scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and its surroundings. It will also release two small satellites, known as 'CubeSats', each approximately the size of a shoebox, to gather additional observations from much closer distances. The investigation is expected to eventually include landing operations.

Together, these measurements should help scientists better understand how asteroids respond to high-speed impacts and improve predictions of how future deflection attempts might work.

Anyone interested in following Hera's journey can explore the mission through the Hera Space Companion. More than a conventional AI chatbot, this interactive communication platform is connected to the mission and designed to make the European Space Agency's first planetary defense mission accessible to the public.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"We just don't have enough people, and we're looking for more," one NASA astronaut told Space.com.

If NASA ever hopes to build a permanent moon base for astronauts, let alone aim for Mars, the U.S. space agency is going to need a whole lot of space travelers. And now, you have a chance to be one of them.

NASA on Saturday (Nov. 7) put out the call for a new class of astronaut candidates who think they have the "right stuff" to fly, live and work in space. Those astronaut hopefuls have until Dec. 3 to apply (the application website is here), with NASA planning to make its final selections in late 2027.

"This is an extraordinary time to join NASA's astronaut corps," the space agency's chief, Jared Isaacman, said in an announcement, which was made during NASA's "Max Power" air show at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida. "The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars."

It's been two years since NASA last sought applications for astronauts. In 2024, more than 8,000 people applied, though only 10 — five men and five women — made the cut. They're in the middle of a two-year training program right now.

This new 2027 astronaut group will be the 25th astronaut class in NASA history. Its announcement comes the same year that NASA returned astronauts to the moon for the first time since the Apollo era with the Artemis II moon flyby. Four more astronauts will test Artemis moon landers in Earth orbit on the Artemis III mission in 2027.

NASA currently has 32 active astronauts in its spaceflying corps. The agency has recruited 370 people to fly in space since 1959, when the first seven Mercury astronauts were selected and unveiled to the world.

"There is a lot to be done in order to get all of these new vehicles and the new suits and everything as we continue to work towards the moon, build a base there, stay permanently, and then eventually onto Mars," NASA astronaut Nichole Stilwell, class of 2021, told Space.com in an interview at KSC during the Max Power event. "And so we just don't have enough people, and we're looking for more."

If you're interested in applying to be a NASA astronaut, you should take a look at the requirements first.

NASA's core guidelines require applicants to be U.S. citizens and have a master's degree in a STEM field like "engineering, biological science, physical science, or computer science from an accredited institution," the space agency said in a statement. You'll also need at least three years of experience in your related field.

Don't have a master's degree? Here's three other ways NASA might consider your application, according to the agency's advisory:

If you're a medical doctor and are considering applying to be an astronaut, your residency training can be counted toward your professional experience, but only if it is completed by July 2027, NASA said.

If you want to be a pilot astronaut for NASA, you'll need some serious flight hours under your belt. Here's a rundown of some ways to meet that requirement:

"For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said NASA chief astronaut Scott Tingle, who also chairs the Astronaut Selection Board at the agency's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston. "It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space."

Once NASA selects its 2027 astronaut class, the new recruits can expect to begin a two-year training program based out of JSC, which is home to the agency's astronaut corp and Mission Control.

“The window is open. The mission is waiting.," NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson said in a statement. "And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you."

Space.com Content Manager Chelsea Gohd contributed to this report from NASA's Max Power event at the Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

#804. General Hospital’s Randall England Dead at 75

Randall England—who played General Hospital villain Jack Slater in the 1980s—died on Sept. 25 following a battle with esophageal cancer, according to his family. He was 75.

Port Charles is feeling a little bit emptier.

Randall England—who was best known for his role as General Hospital villain Jack Slater during the 1980s—died on Sept. 25 in Los Angeles following a battle with esophageal cancer, according to his family. He was 75.

"Randall had the good fortune of surrounding himself with a wonderfully varied and interesting circle of people," read his online obituary. "Charming, loving, and generous with his time and energy, Randall was someone people could count on."

The tribute continued, "His legacy lives on in the people he loved, taught, and supported."

Born in 1951 in Oklahoma City, Okla., England began his career as a model before studying acting in New York. According to his obituary, a brief trip to Los Angeles for an audition "became a home," with the actor settling down in Beverly Hills.

He was first introduced on General Hospital in 1984, playing a stranger who arrives in Port Charles posing as a film producer. He remained on the soap opera for nearly year before his character was killed off in a dramatic shootout.

In addition to General Hospital, England appeared on iconic TV shows such as Dallas, The Young and the Restless and Baywatch. His other acting credits include 2003's Hellborn, 2008's Beverly Hills Chihuahua and Maroon 5’s 2015 music video for “Sugar.

But, according to England's family, his favorite role was being a dad to daughter Micaela Reed—who he shared with Jennifer Leigh Herreras—as well as "Pappaw" to grandkids Katherine Reed and Julian Reed.

"Friends, family, and former students have remembered his authenticity and the steady presence he offered in their lives," they wrote in his obituary. "He offered encouragement and advice freely."

"He was well known for his fashion sense, with stylish cowboy boots a fixture of his signature uniform for many years," England's family added. "Beverly Hills won’t be the same without him cruising around in his vintage BMW, sporting his dark Ray-Ban sunglasses."

The first trailer for Other World: A Stranger Things Adventure doesn't show much, but there are enough clues for fans to figure out what it's about here.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

So, you thought "Stranger Things" was done and dusted after all that Conformity Gate nonsense? No way! Netflix's sci-fi sensation returns in the live-action prequel series "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure."

Created by the Duffer Brothers and Kate Trefry, with the episodes set to be directed by Joe Wright ("Darkest Hour", "Black Mirror"), this new show isn't set in Hawkins or the electric '80s. No, this time around, the action takes place in Marion, Nevada, in 1955, and you know what else is located in Nevada, right? Area 51.

The teaser trailer certainly teases the possibility of a trip to the world's most paradoxically famous secret military base, showcasing a bike and radio resting outside of a fence with a sign that clearly says it's a restricted area (in any TV show or film, that's actually an invitation to see what's on the other side). Of course, the tease doesn't end there, as the thunder booms in the sky and there's a visual hint of a wormhole.

No story details about "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" have been released to date, but there are some clues out there for all the Internet sleuths.

Trefrey wrote the Henry Creel-focused "Stranger Things: The First Shadow" play, while Matt Duffer explained to Variety how a spin-off show would tackle the rock that Henry found in the briefcase in "Stranger Things." So, yes, expect this to be a Henry-centric affair and the start of his long, hard road to hell and becoming Vecna.

What'll be interesting, though, is to see how the show ties into the history of Area 51. After all, it was on April 12, 1955, that CIA officer Richard Bissell discovered the site, while the "Other Worlds" trailer has the date of April 19th clearly marked onscreen, so the timelines align nicely here.

"Stranger Things" has never been shy of tying itself to real-world science and historical events, so it'll be fascinating to see how the show explores Area 51 as a concept and the secrets everybody believes are hidden there.

Was it really a site to test highly advanced weapons and aircraft, or was E.T.'s cousin held hostage there until he revealed Colonel Sanders' 11 herbs and spices? Who knows, with all this renewed excitement around this mysterious military facility, we might get another "Storm Area 51" event to enjoy and laugh at all over again.

Regardless, more "Stranger Things" is welcome news, and since it's presumably about one of the show's best characters, Henry Creel, it only adds another layer to his already intriguing lore. If we can't have an origin story about Hopper's incredible and envious moustache, this is the next best thing.

"Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" arrives on Netflix in 2028.

#802. Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn

Keeping daylight saving time in effect all year could bring brighter evenings, but new research suggests the change would come with a troubling consequence for American children. A nationwide switch could result in at least 2 billion additional trips to school in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks while reducing children's exposure to important morning sunlight.

The debate over permanent daylight saving time has gained momentum in Washington, D.C. This past summer, the U.S. House of Representatives approved legislation that would eliminate the annual return to standard time in the fall. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already approved measures supporting the change, which would take effect in those states if the federal bill becomes law.

The legislation remains stalled in the Senate, with school start times emerging as a major concern. Permanent daylight saving time (DST) would push sunrise an hour later during the winter months, leaving mornings darker from November through March. Although this would affect everyone traveling early in the day, researchers at the University of Washington wanted to understand what it would mean specifically for children heading to school.

Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Add Billions of Dark School Commutes

To measure the potential impact, the research team examined 14 of the 19 states that have already approved permanent daylight saving time measures. They combined school enrollment figures, individual school start times, and geographic coordinates to determine how frequently students would need to travel to school before sunrise. The researchers then calculated the total number of these trips under the proposed system and compared it with the current practice of changing clocks twice a year.

The results revealed substantial increases. In Washington state alone, permanent daylight saving time would produce nearly 35 million additional school commutes in darkness. Similar patterns emerged across the other 13 states, with Georgia showing the largest increase at approximately 71 million additional dark trips.

When the researchers extended their findings to estimate the nationwide impact, they calculated that permanent daylight saving time would create at least 2 billion more trips to school before sunrise compared with the current system.

The potential consequences go beyond inconvenient mornings. An analysis of U.S. traffic collision records found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely to occur during dark mornings as after sunrise. The findings were published October 29 in the journal Current Biology.

"It's called the 'Sunshine Protection Act' because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act," said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a professor of biology at the University of Washington. "These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It's a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark."

Why Morning Sunlight Matters for Children's Health

Beyond concerns about traffic safety, losing access to morning sunlight could interfere with the body's natural daily rhythms. Bright light early in the day helps synchronize the circadian clock, the internal timing system that influences sleep, mood, appetite, and other important functions. When people receive too little morning light, maintaining these biological rhythms can become more difficult.

For children, who must typically follow fixed school schedules, darker mornings could mean missing a valuable opportunity to receive daylight at a time when their bodies need it.

"When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight," said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral researcher in biology at the University of Washington. "We were asking what's the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school."

The researchers also identified which communities would experience the greatest changes. Schools located near the western boundaries of time zones, including those in Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected because sunrise already occurs relatively late in those locations. Districts that begin classes early in the morning would face similarly large increases in dark commutes.

Mississippi and Alabama offer striking examples. Schools in both states begin, on average, before 8 a.m. Under the current clock system, each state has approximately 2 million school trips in darkness. With permanent daylight saving time, that figure would rise to more than 20 million trips per state.

"Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier."

Why the 2 Billion Estimate May Be Too Low

Although the researchers used detailed school information to calculate changes in 14 states, their nationwide estimate required broader assumptions. To project what would happen if the entire United States adopted permanent daylight saving time, they assumed students would generally be leaving for school at around 8 a.m.

Because many children begin traveling earlier, the team believes the projected increase of approximately 2 billion dark commutes may substantially underestimate the actual impact.

"For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "That's pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number."

The findings also raise questions about efforts to improve teenagers' sleep by delaying high school start times. Adolescents typically have biological clocks that shift later than those of younger children and adults, making later school schedules beneficial. The researchers argue that permanently moving clocks forward could undermine some of those gains by making morning sunlight less accessible.

One possible solution would be to start school later to compensate for the darker mornings. However, de la Iglesia argues that such a change could have ripple effects throughout daily life, potentially requiring families and workplaces to adjust their schedules as well.

"I've heard the argument, 'If we're in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'" de la Iglesia said. "Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we're just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time."

The researchers' findings highlight a central tradeoff in the debate over permanent daylight saving time. While eliminating seasonal clock changes would provide more evening sunlight during winter, the additional daylight would come at the expense of morning light, potentially affecting children's safety, sleep, and daily routines.

Additional study authors include high school student Daniel Zhang and University of Washington biology undergraduates Nirekh Dasika, Alicia Nam, Jessie Lu, Navneet Tumber, Elena Kully-Rivera, Viridian Klei, and Micaela E. Romero.

#801. 'Unfinished business' - Tuchel committed to England

Thomas Tuchel has been England head coach since January 2025

England head coach Thomas Tuchel says he has "no intention" of leaving the job before Euro 2028 regardless of any offers from major clubs.

Tuchel succeeded Gareth Southgate as England boss in 2025 and signed an extension in February until Euro 2028, which will be co-hosted by England.

Manchester United are in advanced talks with USA men's coach Mauricio Pochettino over replacing Michael Carrick as head coach.

The Red Devils will need to activate a release clause in Pochettino's contract to hire the Argentine, believed to be in the region of around Â£7m.

But Tuchel says his contract does not include a release clause and he does not intend to leave his role to return to club management.

"I signed the contract, I want to stay until the Euros," he said. "I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business."

England lost the past two Euros finals under Southgate before Tuchel led the Three Lions to the semi-finals of his first major tournament, this summer's World Cup.

However, the former Bayern Munich, Chelsea and Paris St-Germain boss did say that he would return to club football after seeing out his England contract.

"I miss the 50 matches [a season]," he said.

"I miss the two minutes when everything is done. You go out two minutes before the whistle goes, it's like the best two minutes, everything is done and you're in a full stadium, lights are on and you're just so excited and you're part of it."

England are second in their Nations League group and have two more group games over the coming days.

Tuchel's side host Croatia on Thursday before facing World Cup winners and group leaders Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

#800. Lily Tomlin Reveals Dolly Parton’s Surprising 9 to 5 Preparation

Lily Tomlin exclusively shared with E! News what she remembered most from working with the late Dolly Parton on 1980's 9 to 5: "She hit with all chargers blazing."

Lily Tomlin will always love her time with Dolly Parton.

Over two months after the country legend died at the age of 80 following a brief battle with cancer, Tomlin shared what it was like for her and Jane Fonda to costar with Parton on 9 to 5—especially when it came to how the Grammy winner prepared for her role in the 1980 comedy.

“She came on the set, she'd memorized the whole script because she thought she was supposed to, and she hit with all chargers blazing,” Tomlin told E! News’ Will Marfuggi in an exclusive interview. “Jane and I looked at each other, ‘Dolly is so great.’ And she was. She was great.”

The Grace & Frankie alum—who was joined by friend and Laugh-In creator George Schlatter for the interview—also expressed how grateful she was to have Parton as a friend for so many years, describing what being so close to the “Jolene” singer meant to her.

“It meant the innocence that was totally Dolly,” Tomlin raved. “The absolute perfection that she brought to her look—her everything.”

“That was like out of the genesis of something brilliantly thought out and wholesome, because she was that person,” the 87-year-old continued. “She just delivered the essence of that to the audience.”

As Tomlin mused, it was a feat only Parton could have achieved, quipping that while Parton was “extremely well endowed,” she managed to also be “totally innocent.”

Tomlin added, “You could totally see the innocence in her.”

Of course, her friendship with Parton wasn’t the only Hollywood relationship the Oscar nominee cultivated over the years, as she’s still very close with Schlatter over 50 years after starring on Laugh-In. Their relationship is one she speaks of fondly in the upcoming documentary Sock It to Me: The Legend of George Schlatter, which will be available to rent or buy on all digital platforms beginning Dec. 8.

And for his part, Schlatter is grateful to have cast Tomlin all those years ago.

“You just walked in the room and the room lit up,” he recalled. “The room just elevated into another space where it stayed, and Lily became a major, major part of my life, my career, and my everything.”

“When you think back about that time, it just happened,” the 96-year-old said with amazement. “It was like a magical, magical moment.”

For a look at how more stars fondly remembered Parton after her death, keep reading.

Parton's younger sister shared moving insight into their special bond in her tribute.

"Every Tuesday about this time, before the sun came up and the world was still asleep, she and I, for many years, had our coffee together over the phone," she wrote on social media. "Being little farm girls we've continued to be early risers."

She added, "As she liked to say; 'shoot Tedda, we get more work done before the sun comes up than most folks do all day long!' We would catch up on gossip, as sisters do, and drink coffee and make plans, as it has always been our way"

Cyrus reflected on his longtime friendship with the "Love Is Like a Butterfly" singer.

"I have so many moments and memories with Dolly, it’s hard to know where to start," he explained on Instagram. "Like every little boy, I grew up loving Dolly Parton. She was a part of our lives, on our TV’s, right in our living rooms."

He also recalled a sweet note he received from Parton before her death.

"Dolly recently sent me a beautiful message, telling me she loved me with her whole heart," Cyrus added. "I will always love her in the same way ….. with my whole heart … and I always will."

The "Malibu" singer paid tribute to her godmother as she shared insight into their last conversation.

"The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share," Cyrus wrote on Instagram. "Our most sacred moments were private, andthey'lll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts."

"What I KNOW is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue and be strong. I have an angel by my side," she continued. "I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis."

The "Kentucky Queen" singer shared how Parton supported her after her mom Noami Judd died by suicide in April 2022.

"To imagine a world without @dollyparton is almost unthinkable," she began on Instagram. "The mark she left on music, our culture, and the human spirit is greater than any of us could ever hope to leave behind."

"When Mom passed, Dolly showed up for me in a way I'll never forget," she continued. "That's who she was—she showed up. She was family. She was a light in my life and in the lives of millions of people who may never have had the privilege of knowing her personally, but somehow felt like they did. There will never be another Dolly. I will miss my friend more than words can say."

She ended her tribute with a message to her longtime friend: "From one mountain woman to another, I will always love you."

The Late Night host—who was joined by Parton in 2019—recalled two stories from the country singer's appearance.

"I told her backstage that my three-year-old's favorite song was 'Jolene,'" he explained on Instagram, "and she made me FaceTime so she could sing it to him." "Later she shot a promo for her NBC Christmas special," he continued, "and when she got on a stool wearing her short skirt she said to the audience, 'I gotta be careful or else I'm gonna show y'all my box office!'"

The former Saturday Night Live member praised Parton's joke.

"Too dirty for church, too clean for the bar," he added. "Just like her, it was just right.  What a light."

"I know I speak for many when I state that there is now a void in the heart of Americana... no, the whole world, that may never be filled," the I Dream of Jeannie star wrote on X. "Dolly, words cannot define the enormity of your talent, the breadth of your kindness, the depth of your compassion and the expanse in which your legend will carry on in perpetuity."

She recalled meeting Parton at the Country Music Awards.

"You were not only someone whose smile and presence were larger than life, your heart was even larger," she continued. "I lift my eyes upward and know that while you've left us here, you're singing amongst the angels, assuredly giving the host of Heaven a run for their money."

"Heartbroken to hear about the passing of Dolly Parton," the dancer shared on Instagram. "She was an absolute icon, a true legend not just for her music, but for her spirit, her kindness, her joy, her light."

The Dancing With the Stars pro also detailed working with the country singer and fellow dancers Mark Ballas and Cheryl Burke for a performance of "9 to 5" and "Better Get to Livin'" on the dance competition in 2007.

"I was lucky enough to share the stage with her, something I will never take for granted," he added. "Her music and the way she made people feel will live on forever. Sending love to all she touched. Thank you, Dolly. You will never be forgotten."

"My East Tennessee angel," Ballerini—who narrated part of Parton's 2022 audiobook Run, Rose, Run—began in her Instagram Story, "Thank you for every ounce of magic and butterflies, acceptance and joy, heart and music you brought to this world. We will always love you Dolly."

"Like the rest of the world, my heart sank seeing the news of dear Dolly's passing," she began on Instagram. "She meant so much to so many people for so long. But the "Dark Horse" singer emphasized that Parton had an even bigger heart.

"I had the honor of meeting and singing with her several times. Every time I saw Dolly, she was a pure, sweet (but not saccharine) sassy, cup of joy," she wrote. "Her way of looking at life with a sense of humor has always been an inspiration to me…"

"If there’s someone you wanna look up to and model your life after, it’s Dolly," Perry concluded. "Dolly was glam, funny, and kind as fuck. Her star will forever shine bright and I bet you she’s already remodeling them pearly gates with rhinestones."

"What a wonderful songwriter and singer Dolly was," he praised on X. "She brought so many people together, we will all miss her so much."

"I've known Dolly since the '70s," the Hall & Oates alum explained on X. "Her loss is immeasurable. She was such a kind and genuinely nice person. And I still don't know how she played so well with those long fingernails! What an amazing mystery…"

"There will never be another quite like Dolly Parton," the musical ensemble began on Instagram. "She was the ultimate singer, songwriter, actress, performer, and philanthropist. She filled the world with light and we are so grateful for every second we got to spend with her onstage and off."

"One of the greatest songwriters of all time beautiful radiant butterfly human," the indie singer wrote on Instagram. "I played with her at Newport once and I felt like my chest was on fire. I was so wildly awe struck."

She expressed gratitude to the Grammy winner, adding, "Thank you thank you a million times dolly."

The former Wheel of Fortune host reflected on the first time he crossed paths with the "Jolene" singer.

"When I was hired to join KNBC in Los Angeles, I was flown out from my home in Nashville," he explained on X. "The coach section was overbooked, and I was fortunate to be moved to first class, where my seat mate turned out to be Dolly Parton. Sure was a nice flight. Rest in peace, Miss Dolly."

"An incredible songwriter, an unbelievable entertainer, and just a genuinely good human being," the Canadian rock band wrote on X. "There will only ever be one Dolly Parton, and we were lucky to have her. Rest easy, Dolly."

The "Piano Man" singer shared a tribute on behalf of his entire family, reflecting on the death of "a legend."

"Dolly Parton has transcended time and become one of those iconic artists who is known for just being Dolly, beyond a specific song or moment in time," he wrote on Instagram. "I was one of the lucky ones whose music she covered."

"We will miss her and her presence on this earth," the message continued, "but we will reap all the rewards of her life dedicated to making it a better place."

He also reflected on a recent visit to Parton's amusement park Dollywood.

"Our children looked up to her and knew her music," he added. "The love for Dolly spanned generations. Her work in acknowledging endometriosis before most people knew what it was, and her philanthropic efforts have been inspirational to our family and our foundation."

"RIP Dolly Parton," the singer shared on X. "One of the most incredible talents. inspiring songwriter, incredible woman. what a gift of song you had. heaven gained an angel."

"An honor and a privilege," she wrote on X. "You will be sorely missed, legend. Oh Dolly."

"RIP to Dolly Parton," he wrote on X, "One of the greatest musical and American icons. She championed children, education, kindness and the overall goodness of the human race. Condolences to her family, friends, team and fans."

"I've said often in my life, 'What will the world be without Dolly?'" the country singer wrote on X. "From the time I was a little girl, I wanted to be just like her. At 15 years old, my family uprooted their lives so I could start chasing my dreams, working in the country show at Dollywood."

"Since then, I've had the privilege of not only working with Dolly, but getting to know her," she continued. "She was exactly who we all hoped she would be—kind, funny, gracious, and one of a kind. Heaven got a whole lot sassier, funnier, and brighter today."

Pearce—who starred in Dollywood's Country Crossroads show in the early aughts—shared her committment to Parton's legacy.

As she put it, "I will do my part as a woman in country music to continue carrying the light she shined so brightly for all of us."

"Dolly, there will never be anyone else like you," the actress—who made guest appearances, like Parton, in Hannah Montana—wrote on Instagram. "I am gutted to hear the news. The world will forever be indebted to the good you've done and the legacy you've left. The equilibrium of the earth feels off."

She concluded her tribute with a message to Parton: "Thank you for everything."

"Dolly spent a lifetime reminding children to dream big, and then doing everything she could to help make those dreams possible," the American Idol host wrote on Instagram. "We'll always be grateful that her generosity extended to Seacrest Studios and the patients we serve. The Overboard actress reflecting on her relationship with Parton, alongside a throwback photo of the pair.

"This was the first day I met Dolly," she wrote on Instagram "She was a ray of light! Even then, she was lit up like an angel, a joyful, celestial being. Dolly blessed us all for generations to come. Rest, dear Angel, and, as you said, keep the angels creating music and singing in the heavens."

"There will never be another," the singer wrote on Instagram alongside a video of her singing with Parton. "@dollyparton was who we could all agree on. She was and is such a light."

"

Hathaway also shared a message for the country music icon.

"Dolly," she concluded, "you have always been one of my angels. I will always love you xx"

"I’m honored that I had the privilege to work with you," she continued. "I will treasure that forever. Thank you for your profound impact on the world. You are an angel who has made this world a happier place because of your joyful art. You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully.”

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA has officially launched the Moon Base Student Challenge, asking students to help build humanity's future on the moon. And there's $1 million in prizes up for grabs for the winners.

To build and sustain a base on the moon, NASA will have to solve a myriad of problems. And they're looking to the next generation for help, the space agency's chief Jared Isaacman said Sunday (Nov. 8).

"We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world," Isaacman said. "We're putting 1 million in prizes together to support the best ideas and recognize the teams behind them."

Isaacman made this announcement wearing his blue flight suit from the rocket garden at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center amidst the agency's MAX POWER air show event. Just the day before, he flew fighter jets in that suit and even jumped out of a plane, skydiving into the event. Soon after this announcement, he was flying another fighter plane above the crowd.

The audience for this announcement was filled with students of all ages. Some young children wearing costume spacesuits squeezed as close as they could to the front of the room while teenagers considering their futures listened intently. It was clear that Isaacman's presence and words were landing with this group.

But what moon base challenges does NASA want to see these students tackle? In short, all of them.

"The moon base will allow us to conduct groundbreaking science, test new technologies, and prepare again for where we inevitably go next, which is the red planet," he said. "But before any of that can happen, we have an awful lot of problems that need to be solved."

"We need ways to generate power through the long lunar night. We need to protect our astronauts from that incredibly harsh and dangerous and demanding environment on the surface. We need to move people and equipment around on the surface and support human life three days away from Earth," Isaacman said, illustrating just a few of the big issues that present with the concept of a moon base.

This challenge is open to high school and post-secondary students based in the U.S. For participating students, they will form teams that will work on an idea from one of six different technical topics related to creating and running a moon base. These six topics include power systems, habitats, communications, mobility, life support and astronaut safety.

This will be what Isaacman described as a "multi-phase competition that mirrors how ideas are developed actually in the aerospace industry."

"Teams will first submit concepts, then they're going to refine them, and finalists will have the opportunity to present their solutions directly to NASA leaders and stakeholders," he further explained.

"The prize money is great for sure, but the the real opportunity is to work on problems NASA is actively trying to solve right now, so students don't need to wait to graduation to contribute to that effort," Isaacman added.

Right now, NASA has a long road ahead of them before a moon base is actually built. In mid-2027, the agency is planning to launch its Artemis III mission which will see a crew of four astronauts practice rendezvous maneuvers with two different lunar landers. If all goes to plan, this will be followed by Artemis IV landing humans on the moon's surface for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

The agency is making these big steps forward to not just a crewed return to the moon, but a sustained, long-term return to the moon. However, knowing that a fully-fledged moon base is still firmly in the future, they are banking on the ingenuity, creativity and passion of

If you're a student or know a student interested in participating in this challenge, you can find more information on NASA's website here. Interested students can register until Jan. 25, 2027.

#798. Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots

North Carolina's blueberry growers are facing an emerging threat from a destructive beetle whose larvae feed underground, damaging plant roots and potentially killing blueberry bushes. Scientists have now identified the insect responsible, providing an important first step toward protecting crops from the pest.

A research team at North Carolina State University has confirmed that the culprit is Prionus imbricornus, a species of longhorn beetle distinguished by its long antennae. These wood-boring insects are becoming a growing concern for blueberry producers in the state.

Female beetles generally deposit their eggs in soil near the roots of hardwood trees. After hatching, the larvae feed on the roots, sometimes destroying enough tissue to kill the tree. The larvae can reach an impressive five inches in length, while the adult beetles do not feed.

A Decade-Old Mystery Beneath Blueberry Fields

North Carolina is the first state to document P. imbricornus feeding on blueberry bushes. However, signs of a similar problem have existed for years. Reports of unidentified Prionus larvae damaging blueberry roots date back to 2010, but researchers had struggled to determine which species was responsible.

Part of the challenge was the insects' underground habitat. Because the larvae remain near plant roots, they are difficult to locate and study. Making matters more complicated, larvae from different longhorn beetle species often look remarkably similar, making visual identification unreliable.

According to Kenneth Geisert, a graduate student in NC State's College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and lead author of the study, this uncertainty has made it difficult to develop appropriate pest control strategies.

"Before now, researchers often just assumed the species of Prionus on their commodities based on adult identification," Geisert said. "If that guess was incorrect, it could mean using a treatment strategy that did not line up with the problem and incorrectly associating species and their hosts. For instance, while P. imbricornus attacks roots, another type of longhorn beetle might attack the trunk of a tree, or dead branches. Without knowing which species of beetle you're dealing with and their ecology, incorrect management can cause adverse effects on non-target insects."

To identify the insects, the research team conducted fieldwork at six blueberry farms in North Carolina's Pender, Sampson, Bladen, and New Hanover counties.

The scientists installed black panel traps containing sex pheromones, chemical signals that attract adult beetles. After collecting the insects, they used a DNA identification technique known as genetic barcoding to determine the identity of larvae found in the fields.

This method examines short, standardized sections of DNA and compares them with reference sequences from known species. By matching genetic material from the unidentified larvae with DNA from adult Prionus beetles, the researchers could determine which species was present.

The analysis produced a 98 to 99 percent match with P. imbricornus, confirming the identity of the beetle responsible for the root damage.

A Growing Threat With No Approved Insecticides

Although identifying the pest represents an important breakthrough, it also highlights a serious challenge for blueberry growers.

Lorena Lopez, an assistant extension professor in NC State's Department of Entomology and Plant Pathology and a co-author of the study, explained that the discovery brings both encouraging and troubling news.

"On one hand, it's very important that we know which species we're dealing with," she said. "On the other, North Carolina was the first state to ever report Prionus infestation in blueberries, and there are no insecticides currently labeled against this pest in blueberries."

To help address this problem, Lopez has begun testing insecticides to determine which treatments might effectively control the beetles.

A major focus is finding the best time to apply treatments. By coordinating insecticide applications with the beetles' reproductive cycles, researchers hope to disrupt larval development before the insects can inflict extensive damage on blueberry roots.

If successful, this approach could give farmers a much-needed way to protect their crops against an emerging pest that has remained difficult to identify and manage for more than a decade.

The findings appear in the Journal of Integrated Pest Management in a paper titled "Prionus imbricornis (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae), an emerging pest in North Carolina blueberries." Gareth Powell, an assistant professor at NC State and director of the NCSU Insect Museum, also contributed to the research.
