Jarre, now aged 78, is 22 albums deep in a career that places him at the head of the table for electronic music’s greatest and most influential artists.

Among his masterpieces is debut Oxygene, which this year celebrates its 50th anniversary. To celebrate its milestone, Jarre embarked on a pan-European run of summer concerts, including a performance at Amnesia Ibiza, for the club’s own half-century celebrations, and he appeared as special guest of honor at the 30th edition of Amsterdam Dance Event in October, where he presented the sold-out opening concert, “Oxygene & Beyond: A Sonic Journey Celebrating 30 Years of ADE.”

Born in Lyon, France, Jarre has clocked up career album sales north of 85 million, and was awarded the Commander of the Légion d’Honneur in 2021, France’s highest order of merit. President Emmanuel Macron was on hand for the presentation.

He’s readying the release of a special edition of Oxygene on Nov. 20 through an expanded new partnership with BMG, and the U.S. publication of Machines: A History Of Electronic Music on Nov. 24 via Thames & Hudson.

Anyma launched his all-new live show ÆDEN at his headline set at Coachella 2026, and has since presented it across the globe, including a performance to 65,000 people in Mexico City, and at China’s largest ever electronic headline concert, May 2 in Shanghai.

Tickets for ÆDEN MILLENNIUM will be available on artist presale from Nov. 18 at 2pm GMT (9am ET), with general sale from Nov. 19 at 2pm GMT. More acts for both dates will be announced in due course.

#763. SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism

For nearly 90 years, physicists have divided magnetic materials into two main categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. Now, scientists have confirmed that a third type exists, revealing a previously unrecognized form of magnetic behavior that could lead to major advances in computing and electronics.

The breakthrough comes from a research team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. In a study published in Science, the researchers presented compelling experimental evidence for altermagnetism, a distinct magnetic phase that combines important characteristics of the two traditionally recognized types.

"In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy," explained lead author Daniel Jost, associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. "Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase -- altermagnetism -- is real."

The team focused on manganese telluride (MnTe), a material that had long been classified as an antiferromagnet. Building on earlier research, the scientists identified direct evidence of chirality, a distinctive asymmetry in the material's magnetic structure. This property resembles the way a spiral staircase or screw twists in a particular direction and provides a crucial signature of altermagnetism.

Beyond its importance for fundamental physics, the finding could help researchers develop magnetic materials with properties suited to future technologies, including advanced memory systems, quantum devices, and more energy-efficient data centers.

Understanding the Two Traditional Types of Magnetism

Magnetism is familiar from everyday experiences, whether it is a refrigerator magnet holding up a photograph or a compass aligning with Earth's magnetic field. But the physics behind these effects is far more complicated than it appears.

At the atomic level, magnetism is connected to a quantum property of electrons known as spin. Although spin is not literally an electron rotating like a tiny ball, it behaves in certain ways as though the electron has its own angular momentum. Scientists commonly describe the two possible spin orientations as "up" and "down."

When these spins become organized into particular patterns, a material can exhibit magnetic properties. However, that does not necessarily mean it will produce an externally detectable magnetic field.

In ferromagnetic materials, electron spins align in the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down). Their combined effect produces the familiar magnetic field associated with ordinary magnets. People have used materials with this behavior for thousands of years.

A second category, identified in 1933, works differently. In antiferromagnets, neighboring electron spins point in opposite directions (up-down-up-down). Because the magnetic contributions oppose one another, they cancel out, leaving no overall magnetization.

A Third Type of Magnetism Challenges the Old Rules

For almost nine decades, these two categories provided the basic framework for understanding how magnetic order arises in materials. However, experimental observations in recent years began revealing behavior that neither category could fully explain.

Some materials displayed alternating electron spins and no overall magnetization, just like antiferromagnets. Yet they could also support useful spin currents, a property associated with ferromagnetic behavior. Spin currents allow information to be carried through the spin properties of electrons rather than relying entirely on their electrical charge.

The unusual combination suggested that scientists were dealing with something fundamentally different. In 2022, researchers introduced the term "altermagnets" for materials belonging to this proposed third magnetic class.

The key difference lies in the arrangement of atoms within the material. Altermagnets have alternating spin orientations (up-down-up-down), but the crystal structures surrounding the oppositely aligned spins are rotated relative to one another.

This rotation breaks a form of symmetry that exists in conventional antiferromagnets. Although the distinction is subtle, it can dramatically change how electrons behave, allowing altermagnets to combine properties once considered incompatible.

Scientists Find the Missing Evidence for Altermagnetism

Even as experimental support for altermagnetism accumulated, researchers still needed a decisive way to establish that it represented a genuinely distinct magnetic phase.

"By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real," Jost said, "but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle."

That missing evidence involved chirality, a property sometimes described as "handedness." An object is chiral when its mirror image cannot be perfectly aligned with the original. Human hands provide a simple example: Your left and right hands are mirror images, but a left hand cannot fit properly into a right-handed glove.

In an altermagnet, the unusual arrangement of atoms and electron spins can create this kind of handedness in the material's electronic and magnetic structure. Conventional antiferromagnets do not exhibit the same characteristic chiral signature.

Detecting that difference would provide a powerful way to distinguish a true altermagnet from a material that merely resembles one.

The researchers selected manganese telluride as their test material. For decades, scientists considered it an ordinary antiferromagnet, but more recent studies had raised the possibility that it belonged to the newly proposed category.

Powerful X-Rays Reveal a Hidden Magnetic Signature

To investigate the material's unusual properties, the team conducted experiments at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France. The facility's ID32 beamline produces precisely controlled polarized X-rays, allowing scientists to examine subtle magnetic structures that are otherwise extremely difficult to detect.

The researchers used circularly polarized X-rays, which have electric fields that rotate in either a left-handed or right-handed direction as the light travels. By measuring how the material scattered these two forms of light, they could search for evidence of chirality.

"Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams," explained Jost. "Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way."

The experiment revealed a clear difference in the way manganese telluride interacted with the two X-ray polarizations. This distinctive chiral response was precisely the kind of signal expected from altermagnetism and would not be present in a conventional antiferromagnet.

"This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own," Jost said.

The researchers first performed the experiment in 2024. They returned in early 2025 and repeated the measurements, successfully reproducing the results and strengthening the evidence for the new magnetic phase.

"This technique helped us confirm that manganese telluride was really exhibiting altermagnetic properties," said Rachel Nickel, postdoctoral scientist with ESRF, a co-author who helped design and conduct the experiment on the ID32 beamline. "Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible."

Why Altermagnetism Could Transform Future Computers

The discovery could have important consequences for spintronics, a growing field that seeks to use electron spin to develop more capable electronic devices.

Conventional electronics store and process information primarily by controlling the electrical charge of electrons. Spintronics adds another way to work with information by taking advantage of electron spin as well.

This extra capability could enable devices that operate faster, withstand interference more effectively, and consume substantially less electricity. Such improvements would be especially valuable in computer memory, large data centers, and other technologies that require enormous amounts of information processing.

However, the two traditional types of magnetism present different obstacles that have limited the development of spintronic systems.

"Ferromagnets are too easily influenced by magnetic fields," Jost explained. "If you have a permanent magnet in your pocket and walk by a spintronic device built with ferromagnets, you could start flipping the bits, scrambling the information stored there. Antiferromagnets fix that problem, but they are practically invisible -- so you can't easily read the data stored in them or use them to drive efficient spin currents."

Altermagnets offer a potentially valuable alternative. Like antiferromagnets, their opposing spins produce no overall magnetization, helping protect them against unwanted magnetic interference. At the same time, their unusual electronic structure allows them to generate spin-polarized currents that can be used to retrieve information.

"Altermagnets combine the best of both," Jost said. "They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information. That gives you an additional degree of freedom to work with."

A New Frontier for Quantum Technology and Electronics

Confirming altermagnetism gives scientists a new class of materials to investigate and potentially engineer for technological applications. By combining magnetic stability with the ability to manipulate spin-based information, these materials could help overcome challenges that have held back conventional spintronic devices.

The next step will be learning how to control altermagnetic states using external influences such as light and electricity. Researchers hope that mastering this control will make it possible to design practical devices that take advantage of the unusual magnetic properties.

Although significant development is still needed before these materials can be widely used, the findings establish a stronger experimental foundation for future work on quantum technologies, computer memory, and more efficient data centers.

The research received partial funding from the DOE Office of Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Curiosity Mars rover is sizing up its next dig site on the Red Planet.

The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of the Mars site, informally named "Nazca," as thoroughly as possible before drilling into it.

Curiosity snapped the close-up image on Oct. 18, 2026, using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI). The image shows multiple roughly disk-shaped potential crystal formations at the rover's next drill target.

MAHLI is located on the turret at the end of the rover's robotic arm. It uses an onboard focusing process to make a composite of images of the same target acquired at different positions to focus on multiple features in a single image.

Scientists theorize that the "discs and needles" texture takes its characteristic shape as crystals, or "crystal forms," grow.

The relatively large sizes of the crystal forms at "Nazca" may provide clues about the temperatures at which they grew, as well as information about the abundance of salts and fluids in the area at the time. Complicating this picture, however, is the fact that mineral crystals can be replaced by other minerals after their original crystallization. The new minerals are known as "pseudomorphs," because they have the same shape as the original minerals but not the same composition or molecular structure.

The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of Nazca — which shares its name with an ancient South American civilization that's famous for the large designs it etched into the rock and dirt — before drilling begins. The NASA researchers will then be able to compare the deeper composition to the surface-level composition.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #761. Parkway Drive Drives It ‘HOME’ In Career-Defining Concert Film Shot at Sydney Opera House

The new documentary traces the Australian rockers on their journey from underdog status in the sweaty metal scene to the stage-and-charts juggernauts they are today.

With the rollout this week in cinemas of HOME, Parkway Drive make the rare leap from metalcore to stars of the big screen.

Directed by Allan Hardy (Viva The Underdogs) and Macario De Souza (Bra Boys), and produced by Hype Republic, the documentary traces the Australian rockers on their journey from underdog status in the sweaty metal scene to the stage-and-charts juggernauts they are today.

Its climax, the band’s one-off live concert at the iconic Sydney Opera House in June 2025, backed by a full symphony orchestra. Related Anyma Will Return to the Great Pyramids of Giza In 2027 Ebro & Peter Rosenberg Aren't Buying Ye's 'Comeback' Narrative After Antisemitism: 'It's All Marketing' Yella Beezy Found Guilty in 2020 Murder of Rapper MO3 on a Dallas Highway Explore Billboard See latest videos, charts and news

Parkway Drive has crashed the Billboard 200, collected No. 1s, ARIA Awards, and played the biggest stages on earth. Few moments, if any, compares to the prospect of playing the Sydney Opera House, capturing the moment for posterity, and pulling it off in the face of potential, ghastly failure.

As far as life experiences go, the concert was somewhere between “wild,” “insane” and “surreal,” frontman Winston McCall tells Billboard over a Zoom.

“Playing the Opera House and everything around this movie has literally been the pinnacle of this man’s career,” he says. “There’s nothing that is ordinary in any way, shape, or form, that will ever be able to be repeated as well, and that can recapture the moment and the work that went into doing what we were doing. And the fact that it was a small fraction of time that so much work went into.”

Hardy and De Souza came to the band with the idea. A suggestion, really. The beginning of a tale, without a middle or an end. “They’re like co-conspirators of ours,” he quips. “They were like, ‘hey, we were in contact with the Opera House, and there’s a date that you guys can play if you want to play. There’s one date available. Do you guys want to do it? You’ve got to say yes, now, basically.’”

The date was six months away, rather close for a band with no plan or idea for the production, and which was, at the time, powering through its 20th anniversary tour.

This is the Sydney Opera House. There might just be one shot. Oh, and metalcore bands, they’re not typically booked for this venue.

The self-funded show sold out in three-minutes. Parkway Drive nailed it. The proof is in the film, distributed by Mushroom Studios, and in the forthcoming companion live album. In one memorable moment, McCall abseils 150 feet from a helicopter onto the venue’s famous sails, and onto a platform two feet wide. Small chance of success, whopping chance of failure.

“We got to rehearse once with the orchestra, and that was four hours before we played. So we did a one full dress rehearsal, four hours before the set, went and had dinner and played it again, and then it was done,” he says.

“So, it didn’t even have time to sink in. You’re just like, ‘oh my god, this is incredible, what’s happening? What the f— just went on.’ There’s no other situation like that in our band’s career that we’ve ever had that compares to that kind of thing.”

Conversation turns to new music. Parkway Drive dropped “Sacred” just weeks before the sold-out, black-tie symphonic show at the Opera House. There’s no word on whether “Sacred” will have a parent album. The band’s most recent studio collection, Darker Still, dropped in 2022 and gave Parkway Drive a third consecutive No. 1 on the ARIA Albums Chart, and the ARIA Award for best hard rock / heavy metal album.

“There’s stuff,” McCall says of new Parkway Drive music. “I mean, we’re brewing things.”

Parkway Drive formed in the coastal New South Wales town of Byron Bay in 2003, issuing their debut album two years later. They landed their first top 10 appearance in Australia with 2007’s Horizons, which also hit No. 27 on the Top Heatseekers chart. Then, 2010’s Deep Blue ignited a run which saw the group consecutively chart four titles in the top 40 of the Billboard 200, with 2015’s Ire peaking at No. 29. Ire also rolled to No. 1 on Billboard’s Hard Rock Albums tally.

For now, the HOME film and live recording, which drops Dec. 4 on vinyl, CD and digital formats, should keep fans of Parkway Drive, fans of heavy music, satiated. HOME – Live at the Sydney Opera House (via Parkway Records/Civilians) McCall insists, “it’s literally one of the best live recordings of any band that I’ve ever heard, let alone a band with a symphony behind it.”

HOME got its world premiere Tuesday (Nov. 10) with a special black-tie event at Sydney’s iconic State Theatre, and opens Thursday (Nov. 12) in Sydney and Melbourne, followed by premieres in Los Angeles, New York, London, Berlin and elsewhere. Parkway Drive will rock festival stages around the world next year, including Hellbound II (Australia), Rock For People (Czech Republic), Rock Am Ring and Rock Im Park (Germany), Sweden Rock, Greenfield Festival (Switzerland) and more.

“We’ve got highlights that include headlining the biggest metal festivals on the planet, to playing some of the most remote locations, to seeing some of the wildest sights and meeting some of the most amazing people,” recounts McCall. The HOME concert, however, “you kind of can’t top that.”

#760. Efficient catalyst-controlled C–H arylation of arenes

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Direct arylation of C–H bonds in arenes offers a streamlined alternative to widely used cross-coupling reactions.1 However, native substrates lack the preinstalled functional handles that ordinarily provide both reactivity and control over the site of reaction. Consequently, despite long-standing interest in directly engaging C–H bonds as reactive sites,2–4 the design of general catalysts that deliver high yields across diverse substrate classes while controlling site selectivity remains a challenge.5–12 Here we show that a microenvironment around a prototypical palladium dicarboxylate catalytic site can provide high selectivity for direct arylation of sterically exposed C–H sites, while high efficiency is achieved using an advanced palladium(II) precatalyst and tailored diaryliodonium reagents for selective aryl transfer. The applicability of this system spans from electron-rich to electron-deficient arenes, while electron-neutral benzene, which is often a challenge for C–H arylation, undergoes successive sterically controlled arylations, delivering functionalized polyaryl compounds. In addition to removing the necessity for pre-functionalized substrates, the mild conditions enable direct late-stage C–H arylation and the installation of aryl groups equipped with functionalities that are typically either reactive in traditional cross-coupling catalysis, such as triflates, iodides, and boronate esters, or sensitive to the basic conditions, such as N-hydroxysuccinimide esters. The results emphasize the distinct synthetic value of palladium-catalyzed direct C–H arylation reactions and showcase a catalyst platform that facilitates high yields and control over site-selectivity.

#759. Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

Sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue. New research from Florida International University (FIU) has found that several types of sleep disorders are associated with physical changes in brain regions responsible for attention, motivation, and decision-making. These findings suggest that disrupted sleep may be connected to important differences in the brain's structure.

Published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders. The discoveries could eventually help scientists identify sleep problems earlier and develop treatments tailored to the specific brain systems involved.

What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders

An estimated 50 million to 70 million Americans experience sleep disorders, making them a major public health concern. To investigate their effects on the brain, scientists at FIU's Center for Children and Families combined and analyzed findings from 57 studies that used brain imaging to examine adults.

Rather than focusing on a single condition, the researchers compared several sleep disorders to determine whether they were associated with similar changes in brain structure. This approach, which is still relatively uncommon in sleep research, also allowed the team to identify differences specific to certain disorders.

The analysis focused on two broad groups. The first, known as dyssomnias, includes insomnia and sleep apnea, conditions that interfere with falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting sufficient restorative sleep. The second group, called parasomnias, includes sleepwalking, nightmare disorder, and sleep terrors. These conditions involve unusual events or behaviors that interrupt normal sleep cycles.

"As more people recognize how important sleep is, there's growing urgency to understand what's happening in the brain," said Matthew Sutherland, a cognitive neuroscientist at FIU and senior author of the study. "By bringing together results from many studies, this research gives us a clearer picture of how sleep disorders affect brain structure and function and where we need to focus next."

Sleep Disorders Share Changes in a Critical Brain Region

One of the most striking findings was that both groups of sleep disorders were associated with reductions in the thalamus, a structure deep within the brain that plays a central role in processing information, sustaining attention, and supporting complex thinking.

The researchers identified changes in a specific part of the thalamus called the pulvinar. This region helps the brain direct attention toward important information and manage cognitive control, which allows people to regulate their thoughts and actions while completing tasks.

The affected areas are connected to larger brain networks that help people concentrate, make decisions, and respond to their surroundings. Differences in these systems may help explain why people with sleep disorders often experience slower reaction times, difficulty making decisions, and a greater likelihood of errors or accidents.

"Most research looks at sleep disorders one at a time," said Katharine Crooks, a recent FIU cognitive neuroscience doctoral graduate and lead author of the study. "By looking across many studies, we found shared patterns in the brain that help explain why sleep problems can impact focus, decision-making and everyday functioning. With so many people struggling with sleep, understanding what is happening in the brain is key to finding better interventions, diagnostic tools and personalized treatments."

Sleepwalking and Nightmares Show Additional Brain Differences

Although the researchers discovered common structural patterns across sleep disorders, they also found differences associated specifically with parasomnias.

People with these conditions showed changes in the posterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in motivation, decision-making, and the regulation of emotions. This finding may help explain why disorders such as sleepwalking, recurring nightmares, and sleep terrors can sometimes be accompanied by difficulties with mood, behavior, or emotional control.

In contrast, the analysis did not reveal a consistent pattern of structural changes found exclusively in dyssomnias, the category that includes insomnia and sleep apnea.

Together, these results suggest that different forms of disrupted sleep may be associated with both shared and distinct changes in the brain. The particular regions involved may depend on the nature of the sleep disorder.

Could Brain Imaging Lead to Better Sleep Disorder Treatments?

The findings provide researchers with new clues about the relationship between sleep disorders and the brain systems that support everyday thinking and behavior.

By identifying which regions are associated with particular sleep problems, scientists hope to improve diagnostic methods and develop more personalized interventions. Future treatments could potentially aim not only to improve sleep quality but also to protect the brain networks involved in attention, decision-making, and emotional regulation.

However, an important question remains unanswered. The research identified associations between sleep disorders and differences in brain structure, but it did not establish whether disrupted sleep causes those differences, whether existing brain differences contribute to sleep disorders, or whether both processes occur.

To investigate this relationship further, the FIU team plans to examine individual parasomnias in greater detail, including sleepwalking and REM sleep behavior disorder.

Understanding how these conditions relate to changes in the brain could help researchers develop better ways to recognize, manage, and potentially prevent some of the cognitive and emotional difficulties associated with disrupted sleep.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A robot just played Tinkertoys in space, assembling the first satellite structure ever made without a human touching the controls.

The DARPA-funded project saw a robotic "truss builder" create a reflective antenna using Kapton film, composite fiber tubes and aluminum joints. The implications are huge for future missions, potentially opening up new possibilities to build — or fix — satellites in the final frontier.

"This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space," Sergio Pellegrino, an aerospace and civil engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement on Nov. 5.

The need for such spacecraft will likely rise substantially in the future, as companies assemble giant megaconstellations for cell-phone communications, AI compute and other purposes. Indeed, the ball is already rolling on such ambitious projects, generating enough hype for space startups around the globe to raise a record $20.8 billion in the third quarter of 2026 alone.

Anything that launches aboard a rocket is limited by the size of that vehicle's fairing — the nose cone that protects payloads during their ride to space. In space, however, the ability to stretch out is practically infinite — after taking into account, of course, engineering and financing constraints.

Assembling structures robotically off Earth could therefore be revolutionary, advocates say. And the recent milestone was a step in that direction.

"This work could be useful not only for astronomy and astrophysics, but also for communications and other areas, such as building very large solar arrays for space solar power," said Pellegrino, who's team leader of the truss-building project, a Caltech demonstration mission called Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA).

ASTRA built a 1.4-meter-wide (4.5-foot) structure in orbit. That's an impressive achievement, but it just scratches the surface of what DARPA wants to accomplish via a program it calls Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design, or NOM4D for short.

"NOM4D's objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space," NOM4D Program Manager Andrew Detor said in a Nov. 5 DARPA statement.

"By 'very large,' I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today," Detor added.

ASTRA was a demonstration, allowing researchers to check boxes and identify obstacles before shooting for a bigger goal. And the team did run into issues — specifically, time limitations, which prevented them from building additional sections of the antenna. Still, the researchers were able to prove out the third phase of a larger DARPA project.

Pellegrino's team completed the two previous phases — defining the mission and testing the hardware in a lab — before shipping the ASTRA payload to the spaceflight company Momentus, Inc. for integration into its Vigoride 7 space tug. Vigoride 7 launched on March 30, along with many other payloads, aboard SpaceX's Transporter-16 rideshare mission.

ASTRA flew with two prebuilt sections of a truss, a robotic "manipulator" and parts to make the rest of the truss in space. In brief communication windows totaling 15 minutes a day, engineers sent up commands and checked in on the robot's progress as it picked up things, readied them in the right spot, and performed construction on an assembly plate.

The team overcame many "little surprises" on the way but were not able to finish the entire truss in time. Still, Pellegrino framed the effort as a success.

"Developing a payload of this complexity on such a short timeline was an enormous undertaking for our small team," he said.

Looking into the future, he is hopeful that robots will be able to build larger telescope mirrors for observatories to peer deeper into space, as well as more advanced structures for radio telescopes to listen for distant signals.

NOM4D is also supporting a project from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, but that one will take place at the International Space Station, focusing on how to harden carbon tubes in orbit.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#757. Genesis Owusu Doubles Up at 2026 J Awards

Winners included Vika & Linda, Swapmeet and Ninajirachi.

Genesis Owusu adds to his glittering industry haul with triple j’s J Award for Australian album of the year.

The genre-blurring artist bags the coveted honor for Redstar Wu & The Worldwide Scourge, his third studio album. Dropping in May 2026, Redstar Wu & The Worldwide Scourge debuted at No. 3 on the ARIA Albums Chart — a career best — and topped the Australian Albums Chart and the Vinyl Albums Chart.

Redstar Wu tackles the political, social and economic overwhelm of the last few years, its “soulful, punk-funk electro-rap visionary renders the paranoia and confusion in thrilling, hook-laden tracks that defy neat categorization,” reads a statement from triple j, announcing its annual prize winners. Related Anyma Will Return to the Great Pyramids of Giza In 2027 Ebro & Peter Rosenberg Aren't Buying Ye's 'Comeback' Narrative After Antisemitism: 'It's All Marketing' Yella Beezy Found Guilty in 2020 Murder of Rapper MO3 on a Dallas Highway Explore Genesis Owusu See latest videos, charts and news

The album, however, “doesn’t just rage against dystopia; it optimistically calls to rally people together to overcome forces that tear us apart, offering vigor, hope and imagination in an era where those qualities feel in short supply.”

That’s not all. The Ghana-born, Canberra-raised artist doubles up with the J Award for triple j and rage Australian music video of the year, winning for the clip to “STAMPEDE,” directed by Isaac Brown.

It’s the second time Owusu has won both categories. Previously, he snagged the top award for his debut 2021 album Smiling With No Teeth, and in the same year collected the music video trophy for “The Other Black Dog,” directed by Riley Blakeway.

“We’re incredibly proud to see Genesis Owusu takes home this year’s J Award for album of the year,” comments triple j music director Claire Mooney. “This record is testament to Genesis Owusu’s unmatched and extraordinary creativity, authenticity and ability to create a body of work that is as thought provoking as it is impactful. If there’s one record the world gets to listen to in 2026, I hope it’s this one.”

Since his career erupted with Smiling With No Teeth, Owusu has dominated the awards circuit in Australia like few others. His treasure chest includes the Australian Music Prize, the Vanda & Young Global Songwriting Competition, AIR Awards, and seven ARIAs. He can fill his boots next week at the 2026 ARIA Awards, where he’s nominated in eight categories, equal best on the night with Tame Impala.

Other winners at the 2026 J Awards include ARIA Hall of Fame inducted sibling duo Vika & Linda (Double J Australian artist of the year for Where Do You Come From?), indie act Swapmeet (Unearthed Artist of the Year for Mount Zero), and EDM star Ninajirachi (triple j live act of the year).

All counted, 23 Australian artists and four directors were nominated for the annual J Awards, which celebrate the best Australian music. Winners were announced on air Thursday afternoon, Nov. 12, to kick off Ausmusic Month on triple j, Double J and Unearthed.

#756. Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive

Every human body produces carbon dioxide simply by converting food into energy. Although the amount released by one person may seem small, the combined output of billions of people adds up to an enormous quantity.

A new study led by the University of Bath estimates that carbon dioxide production from human metabolism increased by 74% between 1985 and 2015, reaching 2.05 billion metric tons annually. The researchers found that the dramatic rise was primarily the result of population growth, rather than a substantial increase in how much CO2 each person produces.

The findings could help scientists better understand the global carbon cycle, which describes how carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, oceans, and land. By measuring humanity's contribution more accurately, researchers hope to improve predictions about how well efforts to reduce carbon emissions will work.

Why Human CO2 Emissions Are Different From Fossil Fuels

Despite the enormous numbers, the researchers emphasize that the carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism is fundamentally different from the emissions generated by burning fossil fuels.

When people breathe out CO2, most of that carbon originally came from the food they consumed. Plants absorbed it from the atmosphere relatively recently, meaning it is already circulating through the natural carbon cycle.

Burning coal, oil, and natural gas is different. These fuels contain carbon that has remained trapped underground for millions of years. Burning them releases that long-stored carbon into the atmosphere, adding to the amount of CO2 circulating through the Earth's climate system.

The new research, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, was led by Professor Javier Gonzalez of the University of Bath's Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism.

The team calculated that global CO2 production from human metabolism climbed from 1.18 billion metric tons in 1985 to 2.05 billion metric tons in 2015. More than 60% of that increase could be attributed to the growing number of people worldwide.

"We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven't had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.

"What we've found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be."

How Scientists Measured Humanity's CO2 Production

To estimate how much carbon dioxide people generate, the researchers analyzed thousands of measurements collected from individuals across the human lifespan, from infants to older adults.

These measurements provided information about the CO2 produced by the body during ordinary daily activities. The team then combined those findings with worldwide population figures and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic CO2 production had changed over time.

The results showed that population growth was the dominant factor behind the 74% increase. Changes in the amount of carbon dioxide generated by individual people played a much smaller role.

Accurately measuring this process is important because human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment. Its influence on local carbon measurements can be especially noticeable in densely populated cities and urban areas, where large numbers of people live and work close together.

Understanding these contributions can help researchers develop more complete carbon budgets, which track the sources, movements, and destinations of carbon within the Earth's systems.

Scientists Stress That Breathing Is Not Driving Climate Change

Although the study reveals a surprisingly large amount of CO2 production, its findings should not be interpreted as evidence that human breathing is a major cause of global warming.

The researchers are not recommending that people reduce their physical activity or change their diets to lower the carbon dioxide produced by their bodies. Instead, the goal is to make scientific measurements and calculations of the global carbon cycle more accurate.

Distinguishing between carbon dioxide produced through natural biological processes and carbon released by burning fossil fuels is essential for understanding the planet's changing climate.

Professor Gonzalez emphasized this distinction:

"The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We're not saying that breathing is driving climate change.

"What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO2 people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs."

By establishing a clearer picture of humanity's metabolic CO2 production, the researchers have provided another piece of information scientists can use to track global carbon movements and evaluate strategies for reducing emissions.

#755. Long-time James Bond Producer Barbara Broccoli Named President of U.K.’s National Film and Television School

"With the opening of [NFTS'] Cubby Broccoli Building taking place in January, this is especially meaningful. My father believed in the power of filmmaking," Broccoli said.

Barbara Broccoli has been appointed president of the U.K.’s National Film and Television School (NFTS), and is the first female president in the school’s history.

The prolific producer succeeds Lord David Puttnam, who will take on the honorary role of President Emeritus in recognition of his outstanding contribution to the NFTS and its continued success.

Broccoli is best known for stewarding the James Bond franchise alongside her brother, Michael G. Wilson, after taking the helm from their father, Albert R. “Cubby” Broccoli. The siblings ceded full creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM Studios in a joint-venture deal last year, with the announcement of Daniel Craig’s successor imminent. Related Stories Movies Gal Gadot Tearfully Warns Against Rising Antisemitism at Simon Wiesenthal Center Gala Movies Nicole Kidman to Receive Honorary Cesar Award From French Film Academy

Broccoli’s NFTS appointment “builds on her longstanding relationship with the NFTS and her commitment to championing emerging filmmaking talent,” said the school. “Her in-depth knowledge of the industry, exceptional creative achievements and passion for developing new voices will be invaluable as the school continues to strengthen its position as a world-leading institution for film, television and games training.”

Her presidency also comes ahead of the opening of The Cubby Broccoli Building at the NFTS’ Beaconsfield campus in January 2027, officially named by Barbara earlier this year in honor of her late father.

“It’s a tremendous honour to become President of the National Film and Television School, following in Lord David Puttnam’s footsteps,” said Broccoli. “Having been involved with the NFTS for many years, I have seen first-hand the extraordinary talent it develops and the vital role it plays in shaping the future of our industry. With the opening of The Cubby Broccoli Building taking place in January, this is especially meaningful. My father believed in the power of filmmaking and in giving talented people the opportunity to succeed.”

Puttnam, an Oscar-winning producer whose credits include Chariots of Fire, The Killing Fields and Midnight Express, said: “I could not be happier than to be handing over the Presidency of the NFTS to my close friend Barbara. To leave the school in such good hands is repaying the last of the many debts I owe to my predecessor Richard Attenborough. My long relationship with the school, and the challenges we’ve faced and overcome, has in many ways defined my career. I’d like to pay a special tribute to those many, many colleagues who have helped make the NFTS the most rewarding journey of my life.”

#754. Inside the 2026 Person of the Year Gala Honoring Daddy Yankee: ‘I Couldn’t Believe Everything I Had Built’

J Balvin, Feid, Trueno, The Sugar Hill Gang, and more artists celebrated the pioneering reggaetón star at the intimate event in Las Vegas.

Music stars and industry leaders gathered at the MGM Grand Marquee Ballroom in Las Vegas on Wednesday (Nov. 11) for an evening that honored Daddy Yankee, The Latin Recording Academy’s 2026 Person of the Year.

As tradition holds, the invite-only gala included a dinner and presentation that ran more than three hours, featuring renditions of Daddy Yankee’s repertoire performed by different artists.

“For the first time in history, the Academy honors one of the great pioneers of reggaeton […] Today, we gather to celebrate his career, his music has brought people together—across cultures and generations,” said Manuel Abud, CEO of The Latin Recording Academy, ahead of welcoming the Puerto Rican artist. “Tonight will be a very special journey through your musical career. We have surprises, first-time moments, and music that we believe inspired you.”

The tribute began with a brief introduction by Jorge Drexler and DJ Playero spinning some of Yankee’s earlier hits, before officially starting with a performance by Anthony Ramos singing “Coraza Divina” (2007) in salsa. Immediately after, Tito El Bambino, Jowell y Randy, and Feid gave a euphoric performance of “Gasolina.”

“To me, he is like an older brother,” Tito told the audience of how he was 12 years old when he met Yankee. “He had vision and believed in the new generations. I pray that God grants this gentleman a long life. Thank you for everything you have done for the entire industry.”

One of the most notable moments of the night was when ’80s hip-hop group The Sugar Hill Gang — whom Yankee is a fan of — brought their “Rapper’s Delight” to the stage. In another special moment, the new generation of rappers, J Noa, Paulo Londra, Trueno, Feid, and Ryan Castro, joined forces on a powerful medley that included “Rompe,” “Gangsta Zone,” “Talento de Barrio,” and “Somos de Calle.”

Other artists who formed part of the special ceremony included Reik and Luisa Sonza doing a bossanova version of “Ella Me Levantó”; Farruko, Rawayana, and Kapo performing a reggae version of “La Despedida”; Natalia Jimenez and Pablo Alborán crooning the crowd with a ballad version of “De Vuelta Pa’ La Vuelta;” Tito Nieves, Oscar D’ Leon, and Nathy Peluso giving “Despacito” a salsa twist; and Pedro Capo and Elena Rose’s classical “Ora Por Mi,” to name a few.

Additionally, artists such as Juan Luis Guerra, Fergie, Luis Fonsi, Black Eyes Peas, Carlos Vives, Snow, Lil Jon, Steve Aoki, and others, sent heartfelt video messages.

Following the back-to-back performances, J Balvin and LL Cool J took center stage to recount Yankee’s impactful and lasting career, and welcome him to the stage.

“I am at a loss for words,” Yankee, who was accompanied by his parents, son, and brothers, said during part of his speech. “First, I want to give glory to God — not out of habit, but because if I am standing here today, it is by His grace, not by my own merits. Thank you to the artists who came up to sing my songs… everything turned out incredible. Never in my life have I felt an emotion as powerful as the one I felt today. As I was enjoying the moment and reflecting, I could hardly believe everything I had built. It reminded me that these songs are not mine—they belong to you.”

Yankee wrapped the Person of the Year gala by singing three of his bangers: “Botz,” “Sonríele,” and “Lo Que Paso Paso.”

This April, The Latin Recording Academy revealed DY as this year’s Person of the Year, celebrating his nearly 30-year career that serves as an example of perseverance, resilience and creativity.

Widely recognized for catapulting reggaetón music from an underground genre to a global movement, in large part thanks to his 2004 hit “Gasolina,” from his 2004 album Barrio Fino, which spent 24 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Top Latin Albums chart, the artist born Ramón Luis Ayala Rodríguez has earned over 100 entries—including seven No. 1s—on the Hot Latin Songs chart. Among those hits is “Despacito,” alongside Luis Fonsi, which spent 56 weeks at the top in 2017.

In 2022, he announced his retirement from music and conversion to Christianity, but made a comeback with a renewed faith and commitment to make “music with a purpose” three years later. His faith-based album, Lamento en Baile (2025), includes the feel-good “Sonríele” which peaked at No. 1 on the Billboard Latin Airplay chart last October.

Yankee is currently making the rounds with his new studio album, La Postal that includes collaborations with Cardi B, Myke Towers, Danny Ocean, and others. He is also confirmed as a headliner of the 2027 edition of Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival.

#753. Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot

Scientists have achieved a new world record by producing extraordinarily intense X-ray flashes that last just 300 attoseconds, an almost unimaginably brief period of time. Using the European XFEL, a powerful X-ray research facility, the team concentrated the flashes into an area roughly 100,000 times smaller than the cross-section of a typical human hair.

By squeezing so much X-ray energy into such a tiny space, the researchers created an exceptionally powerful beam that could open new possibilities for studying the behavior of electrons inside atoms and molecules. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists observe the rapid movements of electrons during chemical reactions and potentially even learn to control them.

The experiment took place in April 2026, and the findings have now been published in the scientific journal Optica.

Record-Breaking X-Ray Flashes Last Just 300 Attoseconds

"This is a world record in intensity and fluence for a hard-X-ray attosecond pulse," says Ichiro Inoue from the University of Tokyo, first author of the publication.

Hard X-rays are a form of light with extremely short wavelengths. Scientists use two measurements to describe their extraordinary power. Fluence refers to the amount of energy delivered to a particular area, while intensity also considers how quickly that energy is delivered.

In this experiment, each X-ray pulse lasted an estimated 300 attoseconds (an attosecond is a billionth of a billionth of a second). Such incredibly short flashes offer researchers a way to investigate events that unfold far too quickly for conventional observation.

To concentrate the X-rays, the team used a specialized optical arrangement called an advanced Kirkpatrick-Baez, or AKB, system. It consists of two exceptionally precise mirrors that focus the beam in different directions. Each pulse underwent four reflections in total, with one mirror focusing the X-rays vertically and the other horizontally.

The result was an astonishingly small focal spot measuring just 180 × 330 nanometers (a nanometre is a billionth of a meter). By directing the energy into this microscopic area, the researchers were able to achieve record-breaking intensity.

"A few years ago, we demonstrated terawatt-scale hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL," says DESY scientist Jiawei Yan, one of the corresponding authors of the study. "But generating powerful pulses is only the first step. For experiments, what really matters is what we can deliver to the sample. With this advance, we can now use attosecond X-rays to explore highly nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter."

These nonlinear interactions occur when extremely intense X-rays cause matter to respond in ways that would not normally happen under weaker illumination. Studying such effects could reveal new details about how atoms and electrons behave under extreme conditions.

An Extraordinary Reaction Inside Copper Atoms

To confirm the exceptional intensity of their X-ray pulses, the researchers directed them at a thin sheet of copper. The experiment provided independent evidence that the focused flashes reached peak intensities exceeding 10²⁰ watts per square centimeter.

When the X-rays struck the copper, they knocked electrons out of the atoms' innermost electron shells, leaving behind empty positions known as 'holes'. Electrons from other parts of the atoms then moved into these vacancies, releasing energy in the form of X-ray light.

Under ordinary circumstances, this emitted light travels in many different directions. However, when the incoming X-rays become sufficiently intense, something remarkable happens. The emitted light can stimulate other excited copper atoms to release additional X-rays traveling in the same direction, producing an amplified beam.

Scientists call this phenomenon amplified spontaneous emission, or ASE.

"It is almost magical to see this happening," says Anders Madsen, group leader at the MID instrument, where the study was conducted. "Normal fluorescence goes in all directions, regardless of the direction of the incoming beam. But when the ASE threshold is crossed, you see the light cone starting to condense into the forward direction."

The team also observed another important signature of extreme intensity. As they increased the energy of the X-ray pulses, the amplified signal initially became much stronger. At higher energies, however, the increase slowed and eventually leveled off, a behavior known as saturation.

This pattern is expected only under exceptionally intense X-ray illumination. Its appearance provided additional confirmation of the record intensity calculated from the pulse energy, duration, and size of the focused beam.

A New Way to Explore the Hidden World of Electrons

Beyond setting a world record, the breakthrough could significantly expand scientists' ability to investigate some of nature's fastest processes.

Electrons play a central role in determining how atoms bond together, how molecules interact, and how chemical reactions unfold. Their movements happen on extraordinarily short timescales, making them difficult to observe directly.

By combining ultrashort X-ray flashes with extremely high intensity, researchers hope to capture information about electrons before the incoming radiation has time to substantially alter the material being studied. This could provide a clearer picture of electron behavior inside atoms and molecules and, in the longer term, potentially lead to methods for influencing electron motion during chemical reactions.

The advanced Kirkpatrick-Baez mirror system used for the record-setting experiment was transported from Japan. European XFEL is now preparing to receive its own AKB system, with delivery expected in early 2027.

The new equipment is being funded through a collaboration with the University of Hamburg, with additional support from the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR).

Once the system has been installed and commissioned, scientists from around the world using the MID instrument are expected to gain access to these exceptionally brief and intense X-ray flashes. The upgraded capabilities could allow researchers to investigate electron behavior at a level of detail that has previously been difficult to achieve, bringing them closer to understanding and potentially controlling the fundamental processes behind chemical reactions.

Materials provided by European XFEL. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

At the height of the Cold War, two amateur radio operators alleged they intercepted signals from Soviet cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained secret.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the final weeks of 1960, two young radio enthusiasts were monitoring transmissions from a home-built listening station on a rooftop in Turin, Italy, when the brothers detected something extraordinary: a faint signal that bore the hallmarks of one originating from space. That wasn't the only surprising thing about the alleged signal:, the transmission carried a very familiar message: it was Morse code for the international distress signal SOS.

As the youths listened, the signal seemed to grow weaker. This raised a troubling possibility: could it be that the signal's source was moving farther away from Earth? And if so, was it possible that this concerning signal was of Soviet origin — perhaps a spacecraft drifting helplessly into space, carrying a cosmonaut on board whose doomed mission had never been publicly acknowledged?

These strange events from November 1960 became the first in a series of alleged radio signal interceptions that would form the basis of an enduring Cold War-era mystery involving so-called "lost cosmonauts" — early Soviet space travelers rumored to have died during secret spaceflight missions before Yuri Gagarin's historic flight the following spring, in April 1961.Today, more than six decades later, the story remains one of the most haunting legends of the Space Age. Were there truly early Soviet space missions — with tragically ill-fated cosmonaut crews — that remain undisclosed to this day?

The peculiar story began in October 1957, as the Italian brothers Achille and Gian Battista Judica-Cordiglia learned, along with the rest of the world, about the Soviet Union's successful launch of Sputnik 1, Earth's first artificial satellite.

Immediately, the two became fascinated with the idea of trying to listen in on signals from such spacecraft and began working to assemble their very own radio tracking station, which they put together mostly from secondhand military surplus equipment. What they couldn't easily find and purchase, the brothers would often assemble themselves. They built an improvised tracking station in an abandoned World War Two bunker, which the brothers dubbed Torre Bert, that eventually became a fully functional radio facility with an antenna they built from salvaged materials like chicken wire and scraps of metal.

Whatever it lacked in aesthetics, the station made up for in functionality, and soon the brothers' amateur efforts reportedly allowed them to successfully intercept transmissions associated with Sputnik 2, the first Soviet spacecraft to carry a living creature into orbit: a dog named Laika, who became a one-way passenger on the mission. Later, the boys also said they were able to track transmissions from America's Explorer 1 satellite.

Some of what the Judica-Cordiglia brothers were able to achieve could be chalked up to being in the right place at the right time. Specifically, their location in northern Italy was advantageous, since it allowed them to monitor signals from Soviet spacecraft passing overhead.

By late November 1960, the Judica-Cordiglia brothers learned of reports from a West German observatory suggesting there may have been an unidentified satellite in orbit, raising an intriguing possibility: could there have been a spacecraft launch that had not been disclosed to the public?

Intrigued, the brothers began spending their evenings at Torre Bert scanning the skies for radio frequencies in search of the alleged mystery object. Eventually, they claimed to have detected a signal that differed significantly from those they had tracked in the past. Unlike the familiar electronic beeps they had intercepted from other satellites, this transmission seemed unmistakable: it was Morse code for SOS.

According to their account, as the pair listened to the alarming transmission, the signal gradually began to fade, raising a disconcerting possibility: what if the spacecraft they were monitoring hadn't merely been traveling through orbit, but had been drifting away from Earth?

If correct, the implications were staggering: the Soviet Union may have launched a secret space mission, but this time with a human cosmonaut on board — and something had gone terribly wrong, ending with a spacecraft and its occupant becoming lost in space.

Significantly, the brothers appear to have reached this conclusion independently, and no verified evidence has ever surfaced establishing that the transmission they claimed to have intercepted originated from a crewed spacecraft, let alone one associated with an unacknowledged Soviet mission that somehow escaped Earth's gravitational influence, with tragic results.

Nonetheless, the brothers' claims would soon help give rise to a disturbing possibility: that there had been unknown "lost" cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained hidden from public knowledge.

The alleged distress signal was only the beginning of a series of unsubstantiated claims the Judica-Cordiglia brothers made, and by the first days of February 1961, the amateur radio sleuths would claim to have intercepted another odd signal. This time, the pair claimed to have heard labored breathing coming across the airwaves, and even what resembled the strained moans of a person aboard an orbiting spacecraft.

In an equally eerie recording the brothers produced, what sounded like a rapidly beating human heart could be heard. The brothers shared the recording with Italian cardiologist Achille Dogliotti, whose examination reportedly led him to conclude that the sounds were consistent with strained breathing and an elevated human heartbeat.

With time, more recordings would begin to appear, featuring transmissions the boys believed to be evidence of unsuccessful Soviet missions that preceded the successful spaceflight of Yuri Gagarin, whose 108-minute journey around Earth in 1961 made him the first human to travel into space.

However, what may be the brothers' most controversial claim involved a recording they believed captured the final moments of a female cosmonaut whose ill-fated journey allegedly occurred prior to the historic 1963 spaceflight of Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman to travel into space. However, experts have pointed out that these transmissions do not follow typical military communications protocols, further casting doubt on their legitimacy.

As the Judica-Cordiglia brothers' notoriety increased, journalists and curiosity-seekers weren't the only ones whose attention they reportedly began to attract; their activities also allegedly garnered interest from intelligence officials.

In one instance, the brothers claimed a man identifying himself as a Russian reporter had visited them. Shortly thereafter, another individual — this time claiming to be an Italian counterintelligence agent — warned them that the "journalist" who had come to see them was a KGB agent.

The Judica-Cordiglias and their unconventional hobby, it seemed, had now placed them in the crosshairs of Soviet intelligence officials.

An unusual twist in this part of the Italian brothers' story would eventually emerge decades later, when London-based journalist Kris Hollington began reinvestigating their claims for a feature story that appeared in the paranormal-focused magazine Fortean Times. According to Hollington, a former Soviet KGB operative who later served as a Russian ambassador to a European country had reportedly confirmed (on condition of anonymity) that Moscow was indeed interested in the Judica-Cordiglias and their claims.

"Our cosmonauts were warned to be careful what they said while in space after this and we had the brothers followed," the former KGB agent reportedly told Hollington.

Things could have ended tragically for the brothers if it were not for the fame they achieved at the time for their alleged radio interceptions. As the former KGB agent told Hollington, it was believed for a time that the brothers "had to be dealt with — an accident perhaps," although after they appeared on a television program that brought them significant attention, any Soviet plans that would have endangered the brothers became impractical.

"That saved their lives," the former KGB agent reportedly told Hollington, who expressed gratitude for the circumstances that may well have saved the Italian brothers, with the former agent confiding to Hollington that he thought "they were good kids."

Of course, the claims of alleged Soviet surveillance are difficult to verify given the anonymity requested by Hollington's source. The same must be said of many of the claims made by the Judica-Cordiglias — even if the brothers were successful in intercepting Soviet transmissions at the time, that alone does not prove that they uncovered evidence of unacknowledged missions during which cosmonauts may have perished.

Some, like spaceflight researcher Sven Grahn, have acknowledged the genuine tracking capabilities the brothers possessed while remaining skeptical of the more sensational "lost cosmonaut" claims, suggesting the brothers might have misinterpreted some of the transmissions they recorded.

"I think that the Judica-Cordiglia brothers did run a tracking station and picked up signals from various spacecraft," Grahn said in an assessment of the brothers and their claims. "However, for some reason they thought that they needed sensational stories [to] maintain their image of a 'hot-shot' operation," he adds. "Once they over-interpreted some receptions and made fantastic claims they were 'trapped' and had to continue to produce sensations."

There is also the possibility that the recordings were hoaxes, of course. Whatever the case, there are no independently verified launch records, authenticated communications, or other evidence from the period that provides additional support for what the brothers claimed to have intercepted.

Something that can be verified, however, is the Soviet Union's well-documented secrecy, adding a further layer of complication to matters. As space historian James Oberg has observed, there are verified instances in which Soviet officials altered photographs and records from the early years of human spaceflight, a fact that has perhaps helped fuel rumors about alleged missing cosmonauts. It is also known that the Soviet space program covered up several deadly disasters, such as a launch pad explosion on Oct. 24, 1960 that killed a high-ranking Soviet military officer and at least 100 others. At the time, Soviet state news outlets reported it as a plane crash.

No verified evidence has emerged to support claims of failed, unacknowledged Soviet crewed spaceflights of the kind described in the lost-cosmonaut legends. Yet the Judica-Cordiglia brothers' accounts have drawn attention for decades and remain among the strangest stories in the lore of the early Space Age — a fact that illustrates humanity's enduring fascination with Cold War mysteries and phenomena that exist beyond Earth.

Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

#751. Gang Dong-won, Kim Go-eun to Lead Netflix’s Period Romance-Action Drama ‘The Twilight Between Us’

The show comes from director Kim Won-suk and and writer Park Ji-eun.

Netflix is adding yet another prestige Korean drama to its production slate, greenlighting The Twilight Between Us, a period drama that’s an intriguing mix of romance and action. The show comes from filmmaker Kim Won-suk (When Life Gives You Tangerines, Misaeng: Incomplete Life, Signal, My Mister) and writer Park Ji-eun (Queen of Tears, Crash Landing on You, Legends of the Blue Sea).

Per Netflix, “The Twilight Between Us follows Mu-yeong and Su-ryeon, heirs to two houses locked in a century-long feud, forced into marriage by royal decree — a union intended by the king to end generations of conflict, but one that soon spirals in unforeseen directions.” Related Stories Business Long-time James Bond Producer Barbara Broccoli Named President of U.K.'s National Film and Television School Movies Gal Gadot Tearfully Warns Against Rising Antisemitism at Simon Wiesenthal Center Gala

The drama will star Gang Dong-won as Mu-yeong, “the illegitimate son of the House of Kang, who carries the ominous title “Demon of the North” and lives in obscurity despite his exceptional martial skill and noble heart.” He will star opposite Kim Go-eun as as Su-ryeon, “the only daughter of the House of Han. After failing to become Crown Princess, Su-ryeon finds herself bound by the royal marriage ban — her union with Mu-yeong an unforeseen twist of fate.”

Gang’s previous credits include the films The Priests (2015), A Violent Prosecutor (2016), Master (2016), and Peninsula (2020) and the TV series Tempest (2025). Kim is known for the TV series Cheese in the Trap (2016), Guardian: The Lonely and Great God (2016–2017), Yumi’s Cells (2021–2026), and Little Women (2022) and the films Coin Locker Girl (2015), Hero (2022), and Love in the Big City (2024).

Additionally, Netflix has confirmed production on a new Korean reality competition series that is a spinoff of Culinary Class Wars. Vocal Class Wars, also set for a 2027 release, is, per Netflix, a “vocal survival competition [that] pits “White Singers” — established artists whose names alone define a genre — against “Black Singers,” challengers who erase their names and identities to prove their worth through voice alone.” One imagines they may tinker with the terminology used in the show when it is launched globally.

Vocal Class Wars reunites Kim Hak-min, the producer behind Culinary Class Wars, and Park Sung-hwan, the producer behind Just Makeup’s beauty-survival format, following their previous collaboration on Sing Again.
